4b96870bc084a271: PETALING JAYA: Majlis Perbandaran Taiping (MPT) menafikan dakwaan tiga ekor gajah yang dipindahkan ke sebuah zoo di Jepun didera atau diabaikan.
Yang Dipertua MPT, Akmal Dahalan, berkata tiga ekor gajah itu — Darao, Amoi dan Kelat — berada dalam keadaan sihat dan telah menyesuaikan diri dengan persekitaran baharu di Zoo Tennoji, Osaka.
Jelasnya, tiga ekor gajah itu yang pada mulanya diasingkan susulan pemindahan berkenaan, ditempatkan bersama semula 20 Sept lalu dan bebas bergerak ke seluruh kawasan kurungan di zoo terbabit.

Mengulas kebimbangan yang disuarakan di media sosial berhubung tingkah laku gajah itu, seperti menghayunkan kepala, zoochosis (tingkah laku berulang akibat tekanan) dan episod musth, Akmal menjelaskan tingkah laku sedemikian tidak boleh dikaitkan secara langsung dengan tekanan, kemurungan atau pengabaian.
"Menghayunkan kepala tidak boleh ditafsirkan secara langsung sebagai petanda tekanan kerana ia juga merupakan indikator menunjukkan tingkah laku 'food anticipation' atau menjangkakan makanan.

"Kekerapan episod musth yang dialami Kelat disebabkan penerimaan makanan bergizi tinggi dan lengkap yang disediakan Zoo Tennoji dan kedua-dua tingkah laku ini adalah normal bagi gajah yang dijaga di zoo," katanya dalam kenyataan.
Beliau berkata, Zoo Tennoji sentiasa melaksanakan program pengayaan (enrichment) bagi membantu kesejahteraan dan kesihatan haiwan itu.

"Mereka juga sentiasa memberikan komitmen tinggi untuk memastikan kebajikan, kesihatan, pemakanan, rawatan veterinar, keselamatan serta pengurusan harian gajah dilaksanakan mengikut piawaian dan amalan terbaik antarabangsa."
Pemindahan ini mencetuskan kontroversi sejak gajahitu dihantar ke Jepun awal tahun ini.
MPT menegaskan ia program pertukaran antara zoo yang bersifat bukan komersial dan gajah berkenaan kekal hak milik Zoo Taiping.
bce3b6fa48ee7675: PARIS: The United States will host the inaugural women's football Club World Cup in 2028, FIFA announced Thursday.

"The decision was taken in view of its experience in organising FIFA tournaments, the maturity of its infrastructure and services and the level of stakeholder interest in women's football in the country," world football's governing body said.
The competition will be staged from Jan 5-30, 2028.
It will bring together 16 top-tier clubs from all six continental confederations.

FIFA said the introduction of the tournament marked "a major milestone for the professionalisation and global expansion of the women's club game, giving elite club sides a true world stage to compete on every four years".

Initially slated for 2026, FIFA pushed the inaugural tournament back by two years so it enjoys a clear window following the 2027 women's World Cup and ahead of the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles.
The US has a proven track record of hosting large sporting events, notably staging the men's World Cup earlier this year.--AFP
16dbe370a287c540: Last year, we reported on Red Viper, a Virtual Boy emulator that added a splash of Super Game Boy-style color to Nintendo's famously failed red-on-black "portable" 3D headset from the '90s. Now, a new emulation experiment, VBoy Color, has taken the concept to a higher level, using a tile-based palette system that allows for many more distinct colors in each individual Virtual Boy frame.

Rather than simply replacing the Virtual Boy's four shades of red with four different colors, VBoy Color's readme files explain how the emulator's game-specific Color Packs can assign a distinct four-color palette to each 8x8 tile in a Virtual Boy scene. That means the emulator can differentiate between green pipes, grey platforms, and red brick wall in Mario Clash, for instance, even though all those in-game objects share the same overlapping red hues in the original game.

The Game Boy Color-esque results feel like being transported into an alternate history where Nintendo invested in a full-color display rather than cheaper red LEDs for the Virtual Boy hardware. The increased contrast between differently colored elements is particularly welcome in games like Jack Bros. or Vertical Force, where the original red-on-red display often makes it hard to differentiate the player-character from busy red background elements.
7a583e8252b93e61: PETALING JAYA: The education ministry will use the 2025 scores in the Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) and data from other national and international assessments to identify learning gaps in the education system.
In a written parliamentary reply, education minister Fadhlina Sidek said this data would also be used to determine intervention measures to prioritise in schools.
"The Pisa scores need to be seen as a reminder that education transformation requires continuous effort and consistent improvement.
"We cannot hope for change to take place in the blink of an eye. Nonetheless, we cannot be satisfied with approaches that do not result in the improvements we hoped to see.

"The 2025 Pisa scores are a clear sign that our efforts need to be strengthened," she said in reply to Ngeh Koo Ham (PH-Beruas), who asked why Malaysia's Pisa scores had dropped despite students reportedly performing better in national exams.
While Malaysia's Pisa scores in Mathematics declined, Fadhlina said the nation scored better in Science, showcasing relatively stronger computational problem-solving skills.
"This strength needs to be harnessed while we address the weaknesses identified," she added.
Fadhlina said excelling in Maths was not merely about memorising formulas but understanding concepts and solving problems, which also demands strong linguistic comprehension.
She added that students sitting for Pisa in 2029 must have continuous support starting now, all the way through primary and secondary school.
The minister acknowledged room for improvement in allocating Maths teachers according to school needs, saying she will look into this.
"This is important to ensure students obtain quality teaching in line with the expertise of teachers."

4506792db22d53cf: KUALA LUMPUR: Pardons granted to those convicted over 1MDB-related crimes will have no bearing on the government’s asset recovery efforts, the Dewan Rakyat was told.
Civil claims differ from criminal proceedings in their legal basis and evidentiary requirements, finance minister Anwar Ibrahim said.
Anwar said the government's and 1MDB’s right to continue pursuing civil claims hinges on the basis of their claims, the available evidence and court orders.
“Similarly, any attempt to seize assets must comply with the relevant laws and legal requirements.
“The government remains committed in its efforts to recover 1MDB-linked assets,” he said in a written parliamentary reply.

Anwar said this in response to Howard Lee (PH-Ipoh Timur) who wanted the government to guarantee that recovery of 1MDB-linked assets would not be impacted by developments revolving around any convict’s sentence.

In September, former prime minister Najib Razak was granted a conditional pardon allowing him to serve the remainder of his prison sentence under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028, subject to payment of a RM50 million fine.

Najib, 73, has been serving a reduced six-year prison sentence at Kajang prison after the Federal Territories Pardons Board halved his original 12-year sentence in February 2024. The initial RM210 million fine was also reduced to RM50 million.
He was imprisoned in August 2022 after the Federal Court dismissed his final appeal in the SRC International case.

In December 2025, Najib was convicted of abuse of power and money laundering involving more than RM2 billion linked to 1MDB. He was sentenced to 15 years’ jail and fined RM11.38 billion. He is appealing the conviction.

Earlier this year, then Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission chief Azam Baki said the country could recover another US$2 billion (RM8.16 billion) in assets linked to the 1MDB scandal by the end of next year.
Azam said the assets would be the last of those misappropriated.
As of 2025, Malaysia has recovered RM31.3 billion, or 74.53% of the RM42 billion misappropriated from 1MDB.
61ccf9704a0429dc: COPENHAGEN: Denmark said Thursday it had bought long-range missiles from US and Norwegian manufacturers after announcing a year earlier it would acquire the weapons to deter Russia.

"We have bought two different missile systems: Norwegian strike missiles from Kongsberg, which can in particular be launched from our F-35 fighter jets, and Anthem missiles from the American company Covenant, which can be fired from land," Danish defence minister Jeppe Bruus told a press conference.
Bruus did not specify the number of missiles or the costs, nor when deliveries would begin.

In September 2025, Copenhagen announced it was planning on acquiring long-range missiles capable of reaching targets inside Russia, stressing that the threat from Russia would weigh on Europe for a long time to come.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen at the time called it "a paradigm shift in Danish defence policy".
"We are facing a security situation where no one can predict what will happen tomorrow," Bruus told reporters Thursday.
The minister stressed that this situation required Denmark to possess new military capabilities to strengthen both its own and Nato's collective deterrent force.
Denmark announced it had also signed an agreement with the United States aimed at strengthening maritime cooperation, particularly in the area of shipbuilding.
Russia's ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, condemned the move, calling it an "ill-considered policy".
702c694cf75a6efb: STRASBOURG: Facing US sanctions, the International Criminal Court was on Thursday awarded the European Union's top rights prize, in a show of support that risks upsetting President Donald Trump.

"The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognises the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice," said European Parliament chief Roberta Metsola in announcing the award.
The ICC thanked the European Parliament for giving it the Sakharov Prize "at a time when the Court and its officials face unprecedented challenges."

"Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law," ICC President Tomoko Akane said.

This month, the United States announced sanctions against the ICC aimed at crippling the day-to-day operations of the court, which tries individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
Trump's administration has vowed to dismantle the court "brick by brick", furious that judges have issued an arrest warrant for Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged crimes in Gaza.

The win comes after ex-ICC judge Navi Pillay, who also served as UN rights chief, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize this month – a choice Trump slammed as "disgraceful", arguing the award should have gone to him.

The EU has already thrown its support behind the ICC in the face of the US sanctions – which will come into force in six months – and has said it is "ready to take any necessary measures" to make sure the court can keep working.
"The International Criminal Court must be free to pursue its mission, independently, and without pressure or intimidation," EU chief Ursula von der Leyen posted online after the prize was announced.
Brussels is hoping to use the delay before the sanctions are applied to try to talk the US down, but is also eyeing implementing a "blocking statute" to shield the ICC from Washington.
Set up in 1988 and named after Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, the EU prize is bestowed annually on individuals or organisations to recognise their fight for human rights or democracy.
The ICC was among three finalists this year, alongside Tanzania opposition leader Tundu Lissu and twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, representing those prosecuted by the Iranian government.
The nominees are put forward by the political groupings in the EU and the winner is chosen by senior lawmakers. An award ceremony will be held in December.

Lissu, head of Tanzania's opposition Chadema party, was detained in April 2025. He faces a possible death penalty if convicted of treason for allegedly inciting the public to boycott elections last year.
Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, 21, have respectively been sentenced to death and 36 years in prison for having taken part in anti-government protests in Iran.
Other recent high-profile winners of the Sakharov prize have been Venezuelan opposition chief Maria Corina Machado, deceased Russian Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny and the people of Ukraine.

d2f3689e83e2876e: PETALING JAYA: Kementerian Pendidikan (KPM) sedang menambah baik Polisi Perlindungan Murid agar pelaksanaannya praktikal tanpa menjejaskan matlamat melindungi keselamatan dan kesejahteraan murid.

Menteri Pendidikan Fadhlina Sidek juga berkata sebarang isu atau kebimbangan yang dibangkitkan oleh guru berhubung pelaksanaan polisi itu akan diteliti serta ditangani menerusi saluran pentadbiran yang bersesuaian.

Beliau menjawab soalan Ahmad Johnie Zawawi (GPS-Igan) berhubung status terkini penandatanganan Surat Aku Janji Kepatuhan Polisi Perlindungan Murid Sekolah, serta tindakan KPM terhadap guru yang enggan atau belum menandatanganinya.

dac68d62184ac99e: PETALING JAYA: Kerajaan mempertahankan pelaksanaan caruman wajib Kumpulan Wang Simpanan Pekerja (KWSP) sebanyak 2% bagi pekerja asing, menyifatkannya sebagai langkah seimbang antara menjamin keselamatan sosial pekerja migran dan mengambil kira kos yang ditanggung majikan.
Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim yang juga menteri kewangan berkata, kadar caruman oleh majikan yang mula berkuat kuasa pada Oktober 2025 itu secara relatifnya rendah.
Sekalipun begitu, beliau berkata, langkah tersebut merupakan sebahagian usaha kerajaan memperluas perlindungan sosial kepada semua pekerja di Malaysia, selaras dengan amalan antarabangsa.

"Ia juga bertujuan memberikan simpanan asas kepada pekerja bukan warganegara yang turut menyumbang kepada ekonomi negara, merapatkan jurang kesaksamaan antara pekerja tempatan dan pekerja bukan warganegara bagi memastikan semua pekerja di Malaysia mendapat perlindungan sosial, serta menyokong prinsip keadilan dan keterangkuman dalam sistem persaraan negara," katanya menerusi jawapan bertulis Parlimen.
Anwar berkata, sebanyak 78,129 majikan sudah mula membuat caruman wajib itu bagi 1,754,460 pekerja asing.
Daripada jumlah itu, katanya, sebanyak 67,194 majikan atau 86% terdiri daripada perusahaan kecil dan sederhana (PKS).
Ini merangkumi syarikat pembuatan yang mempunyai sehingga 200 pekerja, atau syarikat sektor perkhidmatan dan sektor lain yang mempunyai sehingga 75 pekerja.
"Perkembangan ini menunjukkan bahawa pelaksanaan caruman mandatori telah mula diterima dan dilaksanakan dalam kalangan majikan, termasuk dalam kalangan PKS," katanya.

"Kerajaan sentiasa mengalu-alukan cadangan daripada semua pihak bagi tujuan penambahbaikan dasar dari semasa ke semasa pada masa akan datang. Kerajaan akan terus memantau keberkesanan inisiatif-inisiatif ini serta melibat urus dengan persatuan dan komuniti PKS, bagi memastikan bantuan yang disediakan sampai kepada perniagaan yang memerlukan."
Beliau berkata demikian menjawab soalan Jimmy Puah (PH-Tebrau) yang bertanyakan sama ada Kementerian Kewangan sedang mempertimbangkan semula ketetapan caruman wajib KWSP bagi pekerja asing.
Pada Julai, Timbalan Perdana Menteri Zahid Hamidi mendakwa kerajaan telah bersetuju untuk mengkaji semula caruman KWSP terbabit bagi meredakan kebimbangan dalam kalangan komuniti perniagaan.
724f1680bfc6d037: KUALA LUMPUR: The two per cent Employees Provident Fund (EPF) contribution rate payable by employers for non-Malaysian workers is relatively low, the Finance Ministry (MoF) said.
The ministry said the rate takes into account the need to balance workers' social protection objectives with the costs borne by employers.
"The government recognises the challenges employers face from rising business costs, particularly small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

"Under the Employees Provident Fund Act 1991, all employers have been required to contribute to the EPF for non-Malaysian workers employed in Malaysia since October 2025," the ministry said in a written parliamentary reply.
The ministry was responding to a question from Jimmy Puah (PH-Tebrau) on measures to ease the burden on SMEs amid rising business costs.
He also asked whether the government would consider requiring foreign workers to bear the full cost of EPF contributions.
MoF said since mandatory contributions were introduced in October 2025, a total of 78,129 employers have contributed to the EPF for 1,754,460 non-Malaysian workers.

"Of these employers, 86 per cent, or 67,194, were SMEs, defined as businesses with no more than 200 employees in the manufacturing sector and no more than 75 employees in the services and other sectors.
"This indicates that the mandatory contribution requirement has begun to gain acceptance and is being implemented by employers, including SMEs," it said.
The ministry said mandatory EPF contributions formed part of the government's efforts to expand social protection coverage to all workers in Malaysia, in line with international practices.
It added that the government remained open to proposals from all parties to improve policies over time.
"The government will continue to monitor the effectiveness of these initiatives and engage with SME associations and communities to ensure that assistance reaches businesses in need," it said.
4ae9cfff4110700d: PETALING JAYA: The education ministry is reviewing the implementation of its student protection policy, including undertaking forms opposed by stakeholders over concerns about their potential implications for teachers.
In a written parliamentary reply, education minister Fadhlina Sidek said the review would take into account feedback from those implementing the policy and other stakeholders.

"This is important to ensure its implementation is clear, practical and does not cause confusion among teachers, school staff, external parties and other stakeholders, without compromising the policy's main objective of protecting students' safety and wellbeing."

Previously, the National Union of the Teaching Profession (NUTP) voiced opposition to the policy, particularly the requirement for teachers to sign an undertaking form confirming their compliance with the policy.
Teachers had expressed concern that this would put an unfair amount of responsibility on them to protect the wellbeing of students while exposing them to legal implications.
Fadhlina said teachers who had yet to sign or refused to sign the undertaking would first be given explanations about its purpose, scope and implementation.
Issues or concerns raised by teachers will be examined and addressed through administrative channels, she added.

She was replying to Ahmad Johnie Zawawi (GPS-Igan), who asked how many teachers had signed or refused to sign the undertaking, and whether action would be taken against teachers who did not sign the document.
Fadhlina did not disclose the figures requested or whether disciplinary action would be taken.
195eccfad0f57dc7: PETALING JAYA: The Taiping Municipal Council has denied claims that three elephants transferred to a zoo in Japan have been abused or neglected.
Council president Akmal Dahalan said the three elephants — Darao, Amoi and Kelat — were in good health and had become used to the new environment at the Tennoji Zoo in Osaka.
In a statement, he said they were placed together again on Sept 20, after initially being isolated following the transfer and have been given free access to the entire enclosure at the zoo.

Responding to concerns on social media over the elephants depicting behaviour such as head swaying, zoochosis and musth episodes, Akmal said such behaviours cannot be directly linked to stress, depression or neglect.

"Head swaying is also a typical behaviour when elephants anticipate food. On the other hand, the frequent episodes of musth experienced by Kelat is caused by the animal being fed highly nutritious food.

The transfer has been the subject of controversy since the elephants were sent to Japan earlier this year.

61543785573e358a: YEREVAN: Nearly all of the world's shallow-water coral reefs face an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075 due to climate change, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned Thursday.
In the first global assessment of its kind, the world authority on threatened wildlife classified 96 percent of the planet's coral reef systems as "critically endangered" – its highest risk category.
Corals are heat sensitive and particularly vulnerable to human-driven climate change, which is warming the world's oceans and increasing the frequency and intensity of damaging bleaching events.

"The future threat of climate change is looming and severe, and that poses a very high risk to the survival of these ecosystems," said Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.

The emergence this year of a "super" El Nino, the natural warming phenomenon, also presents a risk to corals, Gudka said at a news conference at the UN's COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia.
The IUCN presented its findings at COP17, where governments are under pressure to make progress on a landmark pact to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.
For its assessment, the IUCN used the "middle-of-the-road" scenario from the UN's panel of climate experts that projects global temperatures rising 2.7C above pre-industrial levels by 2100.
The world is on track for 2.6C warming this century under current global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions, the United Nations warned Wednesday.
"Heat stress from climate change is the single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide," the IUCN said in a statement.
Overfishing is also hurting corals as certain herbivores and predators help control algae and maintain an ecological balance, the organisation said.
The overexploitation of parrotfish and other groupers threatens 63 per cent of coral reef ecosystems.
Coastal development, pollution, tourism and more frequent storms are among other threats.
The IUCN's analysis examined 127 tropical and subtropical coral systems covering 188,362 square kilometres.

The world's largest and most biodiverse coral reefs are among those classified as critically endangered – Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in southeast Asia and the western Pacific, the Caribbean's Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System, and the Red Sea coral reefs.
A reef ecosystem collapses when hard corals – which build its living foundation – largely disappear and are replaced by algae, rubble and sponges.

A study published in the journal Nature last week found that, by 2020, nearly half of coral species were at "elevated relative risk of extinction", with climate change the main driver of this decline.
Despite its warning, the IUCN said coral reefs in most parts of the world "are not yet lost."

If scientists look only at what has happened over the past 50 years, excluding future climate projections, 24 per cent of coral reef ecosystems would be deemed critically endangered instead of 96 per cent, the IUCN said.

"This gives us a critical window for action for us to scale up conservation efforts and climate action to prevent the worst outcomes from occurring," said Gudka, who is also research director at Coastal Oceans Research and Development in the Indian Ocean (CORDIO) East Africa, a conservation organisation.

"The actions we take over the next few years will determine what these ecosystems look like at the end of the century, whether they persist as we have known them, or whether they transform into a different ecosystem, which is worth less to both nature and people," he said.
IUCN Director General Grethel Aguilar said it was "not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover."

"We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them," he said in a statement.

"Kelangsungan kerajaan negeri bergantung pada tiga faktor iaitu budi bicara raja Perlis, pendirian PAS dan hasil rayuan dalaman Bersatu," katanya.

abfcbfb60201c537: In a world full of cyber risk, account takeover has emerged as one of the most insidious of all threats. If an attacker can successfully compromise a legitimate email account, they are then able to pose as a trusted individual or organization without triggering any warnings. Traditional email security will see nothing wrong. From there the threat actor can pick their moment to cause havoc with objectives that range from stealing money, expropriating sensitive data and propagating catastrophic malware. Serious financial loss and a damaged corporate reputation are commonplace outcomes.

The typical account takeover lifecycle starts with the bad guys obtaining credentials, usually through the medium of phishing. Generative AI (GenAI) has made it easy for an attacker to trick an unwary individual into giving away login data, perhaps by posing as a colleague or other trusted party or by encouraging them to enter confidential information on a fake login page.

You might expect, once a legitimate identity has been successfully compromised, that all hell would immediately break loose. These days the typical account takeover artist is more stealthy and sinister than that, in no rush to act at this early stage since no alarm bells have been triggered. Most will take their time to test out and verify their stolen login data, and see where it might take them.

“Conventionally attackers would take over an account and immediately start firing off spam and phishing,” says Dave Baggett, SVP Cybersecurity with software developer Kaseya. “Now they are starting to get clever. They’ll get access to an account and sit tight, watching all the email traffic passing and waiting for an opportune moment to inject themselves into the conversation.”
From the inside out

Once they’ve figured out an organisation’s weak points and come up with a plan of attack, the bad guys will start to weaponize the compromised email account to target other employees and internal systems. Assuming their motivation is financial, they might be on the hunt for a way into payroll or invoicing databases. But their ultimate aim might lie further afield in the form of the organisation’s customers and suppliers, and that’s when the real nightmare can start. So called outbound phishing offers the criminal a way to assert control over a whole new range of sensitive end points.

Victims of outbound phishing are highly vulnerable in the face of what seem to be messages from a trusted partner and ally. It is one thing for an organisation to protect its own email accounts with robust controls like multifactor authentication (MFA), but no one has control over the authentication practices of other parties: “Let’s say we have a customer who we’re protecting,” explains Baggett. “They’re safe, but imagine that they start getting suspicious emails from a third party. Our customer has no idea what is or isn’t protecting that third party. Emails coming from that source might appear to be from a real account, but it could be a hacker typing them.”

Given that you can’t run checks on third party organisations, something more sophisticated than regular email security is required. Ideally this would be a GenAI-powered solution that can bring language understanding to bear, able to examine conversation histories in depth to see if something anomalous can be spotted.

It makes life even harder for defenders when the bad actor has successfully assumed the identity of somebody senior. If they are impersonating a top-tier manager with an extensive and trusted reputation then they have a powerful asset on their hands. All the trust and goodwill of that senior individual is now inherited by the criminal.

Conventional email filtering systems will often be configured to allow senior personnel past certain defensive layers with minimal friction, so as not to restrict important business communications. Recipients of mail from such sources may be disinclined to challenge and report them, should suspicions be raised by the nature of what they are asking for. It takes a bold employee to call out as fraud what seems to be a message from somebody at C-level, especially when the email system has apparently green lighted it as authentic.
Bringing the power of AI to bear

The heat is on not just for IT departments but for MSPs who have multiple organisations under their protection, many of which will have no real in-house security knowledge of their own. Kaseya’s own research shows just how exposed many are. New approaches are needed that deal with the menace of account takeover before damage can be caused. And should a takeover transpire, consideration must be given to containing its impact before vital data and infrastructure are affected.

The good news is that modern tools exist that perform just these tasks. INKY is Kaseya's generative AI-driven email analysis tool. It has capabilities that go well beyond any kind of traditional email security, tuned to detect, through the most subtle and marginal signs, when an email conversation is in the process of being infiltrated.

Using techniques such as advanced sender profiling, stylometry and machine learning, INKY is adept at identifying inconsistencies between the known writing patterns of a legitimate employee and the slightly unfamiliar tone of a fake message. It can sniff out that something is wrong, even when message headers seem real, just by spotting the kind of contextual anomalies that expose a phoney message.

INKY is especially useful when it comes to third party account takeover. It achieves this by building and maintaining detailed profiles of trusted senders based on technical and behavioural characteristics. Over time it learns what “normal” looks like and can see when a third-party email doesn’t match a sender’s established profile.
Containing an attack

If a takeover attempt has been successful, there’s more to stemming the damage than just putting a block on a suspect account. By the time of its discovery, a compromised identity may have already led to inroads being made into connected SaaS apps, cloud storage and collaboration tools, widening the possible blast zone well beyond a single email thread.

Modern IT environments are a jungle of identity-driven endpoints and gateways, and therefore increasingly difficult to defend against intruders armed with legitimate credentials. To compound matters, when the bad guys have AI at their disposal they are able to treat these SaaS-driven ecosystems as a single attack surface. Defence that relies on a patchwork of individual tools, each created to solve a particular challenge in one silo of the organisation, will not be up to countering this kind of threat.

That’s why INKY is configured to work with Kaseya SaaS Alerts, a cloud-based detection and response platform designed to help MSPs and others to monitor and protect business applications. Once INKY has picked up that a mailbox has been hijacked, it isolates the user and blocks outbound mail. It then sends an event to SaaS Alerts so that it can lock down that user's access across the rest of the stack. The tools work as a team, INKY blocking the compromised account and SaaS Alerts preventing the damage from spreading.

The power of this partnership comes from INKY’s ability to stream real-time email security telemetry into SaaS Alerts, including inbound analysis results and threat detections, user-reported phishing activity and outbound mail protection events. This type of integration helps to automate real-time threat detection across a complex SaaS ecosystem.
“It means if we see suspicious mail going out, we can shut the account down, and take other remedial actions,” says Baggett. “The more you understand the meaning of the mail, the more you can catch.”
Smart tools to the rescue

The battle against account takeover is never won, and future innovation is always needed. We’ve seen how AI is a dangerous weapon in the hands of the attacker. It’s also a very handy tool for the defender – but there are some qualifications: “You can’t just put every inbound and outbound mail through an LLM since the economics don’t add up,” points out Baggett. “You’ve got to be more clever than that.”

One of the most important and cleverest emerging uses for GenAI lies in not simply protecting against account takeover but predicting where weakness might lie, helping to stop a problem before it happens. Baggett believes that the security industry is at the very beginning of being able to use models to predict in this way. An essential preliminary is making sure the many different components that go into securing an organisation can share information with each other.

That integration work is underway, an early example being the real time dialogue between INKY Mail Protection System and SaaS Alerts. Next step is a unified data layer where any security component can publish an event in real time, and any other component can subscribe.

“We’ll continue to make more integrations of this sort over time,” promises Baggett. “We’re also building a centralised capability for AI. With so many of the different components having their own AI, you need an underpinning platform. We also have a service bureau of Machine Learning experts who can make customised models for different tasks. There’s no sleeping on the job. The volume of attacks is clearly going to increase.”

a492b28d6c95cc14: Researchers in Singapore have developed an electronic fabric they claim can be woven into garments to create a new form of graphical user interface (GUI), for people who find retrieving a device from their pocket too much effort.

The development could lead - at some point - to a "future in which clothing functions as a pervasive, multimodal human–computer interface," according to the study published in peer-reviewed science journal Nature this week.

The paper shows someone interacting with computing devices using the sleeve of a wool sweater (no jokes about the Windows ugly sweater please, this is serious). The researchers, led by Singapore National University research engineer Fu Heng, claim this is a big leap forward.

“This fiber-centric approach shifts wearable electronics from flexible panels toward truly textile-native architectures, laying the groundwork for fabrics that visualize, sense, communicate and compute as naturally as the garments they inhabit,” the paper says.

The researchers claim to have developed a scalable process to make millimeter-thick fibers. Using lasers to strip the insulation from specific spots on the thin copper wires, they attached light-emitting chips to the exposed sections, creating electrical connections to the chips. Thousands of chips were connected to the wires with extreme precision using this process.
The fibers were then fed into a transparent plastic tube, and made pressure-sensitive by adding two strips of a compressible, conductive polymer into a second longitudinal channel in the tube.

The paper says they could make fibers 10 meters long using this method, and that they are thin and flexible enough to be woven into or attached to fabrics. The researchers were also able to add "peripherals" such as a microphone, a speaker, a temperature sensor and a light sensor.

The researchers reckon they could build into the sleeve of a sweater an interactive interface with audio-video playback, wireless data exchange, computing, and dynamic graphics. The fabric can survive 50 gentle machine washes and 1,000 bending cycles without losing its functionality, we're told.

In an accompanying article, Shanshan Yao, assistant professor at the Department of Mechanical Engineering, Stony Brook University, said the main advance lay in building functionality directly into fiber, which were then assembled into a fabric.

“If the fibers prove to be compatible with standard industrial weaving, knitting and embroidery processes, the findings would pave the way to producing multifunctional electronic textiles in almost any shape or size,” she said.

"The work is also a big step towards replacing rigid displays with fully integrated wearable interfaces, moving everyday computing away from flat screens to fabrics that comfortably conform to the human body. The interactive features of the GUI that have been demonstrated so far are relatively simple, comparable to those of early-generation smartphones and tablets," she said.
However, the current prototype relies on separate microcontroller circuits connected to the fibers through cables, and external battery packs to supply power, she pointed out.

"Future research should focus on integrating the control electronics more seamlessly to improve wearability, and on integrating flexible, energy-harvesting threads that can generate power from body heat or movement," she added. ®

e2397a48d3d66e17: Jensen Huang wants the world to stop fretting about AI and start building with it. At Nvidia's GTC event in Berlin, he dismissed predictions of human extinction, defended AI's job prospects, and pitched a $4,000 computer as the family robot.
The Nvidia chief's relentless optimism occasionally gave way to irritation during a question-and-answer session.

"If we don't describe a future worthy to be part of, then we're not going to lead people there," he said. "We have to describe a future worthy of creating. We have to describe a future not of fear, but of optimism. Who wants to create a future that's worse than today's? We don't have to work hard to create a future worse than today. We just let it happen, isn't that right?"

Huang said that we still have to ask the hard questions about safety and jobs, but "it's important, of course, that we don't make it up. It is not helpful in describing an optimistic future when you say that it will be the end of the human civilization. First of all, it's not true. It's made up. I know it gets headlines," he said, dismissing such stories as clickbait.

When asked if AI really makes people more productive, he explained that there are two ways to think about that: either it helps you do the same old thing more efficiently, or it helps you do things you couldn't before.

"Most of engineering, most of design, has to do with exploring options. Try, experiment, try and experiment, iterate, experiment, iterate," he said. "What's the best combination? And you can only have so much time to try different versions. Now I have AI to go off and explore that universe. That is productivity. And inside our company, we do this every single day now. We're exploring the universe of design options that are within the constraints that we care about, that are physical or realistic constraints."
Huang pointed to construction and infrastructure work generated by the AI datacenter boom.

"Construction workers, plumbers, electricians, networking engineers, all of those incredible jobs are being created in the United States. I think it already has created a million jobs, and then the layer above that, look at all the startups that are being created," he claimed. "That's productivity, increasing the GDP, increasing our growth, which also results in increasing how busy we are. But that's the end. AI makes jobs, and hopefully doesn't take jobs."

Asked about people already losing work to AI - global financial services group Barclays Bank said only this morning it is chopping 5,000 workers and relying more on AI - Huang argued that technological change has always displaced some jobs while creating others.

"Now, with AI, of course, some jobs are not necessary as much as before, or maybe not as interesting as before. And some new jobs and new companies and new businesses are necessary. It's the nature of the world," he stated.
On safety, Huang pointed to Nvidia's OpenShell sandbox technology, designed to restrict agents to the resources needed for a task. "If you're making an omelette, you don't need a hammer," he said.

But he got hot under the collar when asked about slowing down the pace of AI development while the risks were evaluated, in light of incidents such as AI agents from Anthropic and OpenAI breaking into other computer systems.
"You would favor pacing the frontier? I favor them doing whatever they need to do to not bring harm to society," Huang said.

"You, sir, if you believe that you should not leave your house because you're inappropriately dressed, or somehow you're going to bring harm to society, could you please not come out?" he told the questioner.

"The message from the labs is that there's a collective action problem, and that some minimum standards in coordination would be good here. That's a different question. If you know something is already delivering harm, you got to stop running," he added.

Nvidia has a commercial interest in keeping the AI build-out moving. It reported $215.9 billion in revenue for fiscal 2026 and $120 billion in net profit. In the first half of its fiscal 2027, those net profits were already close to the prior year's . The opportunity isn't limited to just chips either. Huang put the price of licensing Nvidia's software stack at about $2,000 per GPU annually.
The CEO's domestic vision was also on show. Asked when households could run large AI models, he held up a DGX Spark system.

"This computer has a chip called N1X inside, and N1X has 128 gigabytes of memory… It's $4,000. You're right. It's quite expensive. However, that computer was designed to sit on the network in your house, and it would have agents that are used by all of your family members. So it's kind of like a TV. It's sitting in your house. It's shared by everyone, and everybody's agents will be running on DGX Spark," he explained.
As an example, Huang said his home agent had researched Berlin's best schnitzel and produced a brochure with restaurant pictures and menus.

"So that agent, you know, that computer will become essentially your family's robot. It has no arms and legs, but it's an agent, so it's kind of like a robot. And this one is just for your home. So that's kind of how I see the future. This is pretty affordable. This is a personal computer."
Affordable if your net worth is around $180-$190 billion. Maybe not to the average household struggling to pay bills in a cost of living crisis. ®
ce2a77e6ae8a20da: GREENVILLE, Oct 22 — Young students attending their debut political gathering, longtime supporters coming since 2015, or curious onlookers witnessing a presidential spectacle, they all agree: as Donald Trump runs his final campaign, no one will be able to replace his rallies.
“There’s a lot of Americana. There’s a lot of, you know, happy people,” a Trump fan named Bart said Tuesday night’s outdoor campaign event in Greenville, North Carolina.
Trump has been barnstorming across multiple US states ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, with his party at serious risk of losing their majorities in Congress.
In this rural corner of the eastern United States, “we don’t have stuff like this happen very often,” said Bart, attending with his wife Courtney and their two children, ages 10 and 12.
Bart, who declined to give his last name, walked past a “MAGA” souvenir stand and rows of red, white and blue bunting before finding his seat on an airport tarmac where the rally was held.
It was a familiar feeling. He attended his first Trump campaign event in 2015.

Since then, millions of Americans have experienced this in-person ritual—a unique blend of provocative verbal attacks, consummate showmanship, and tireless enthusiasm, all from a president who has reached age 80.
Low-flying Air Force One
For 18-year-old Jaycie Bullard, dressed in Republican red, attending the rally was a no-brainer.
“When I heard that he was coming to Greenville, I knew I had to come,” said the nursing student enrolled at a nearby university.
“It’s pure joy, I feel like a little kid on Christmas.”
After an hours-long wait, a plane flew low overhead: Trump had arrived. He strode onstage to the strains of “God Bless the USA,” which has become a core part of his political events.

The president launched fierce attacks—sometimes tinged with racist overtones—against his opponents, claimed against all evidence that he won the 2020 election, and cracked oft-repeated jokes before he yielded the stage to a local Republican US Senate candidate.
His rambling, repetitive Greenville speech clocked in at 111 minutes. As always, he left the stage to the Village People’s “Y.M.C.A.”
But these moments, celebrated by the “Make America Great Again” faithful, are the vestiges of a fading political traveling roadshow that only Trump has been able to pull off.
The crowds and venues are getting smaller. Trump, constitutionally barred from a third term, must step down in January 2029.
“I’m nervous for the future,” admitted retiree Patty Laronde, who was seeing Trump for the first time.
“Who’s going to take his place?” she said. “I’m hopeful with JD Vance,” the vice president widely seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate.
Turning politics into ‘entertainment’

Even if another such master of ceremonies emerges in American politics, David, a self-employed 51-year-old, vocalized what many attendees were likely thinking: “the copy is never as good as the original.”
“He is an anomaly,” added Troy, 59, a manager who also did not give his last name. “There’s... never been a president like him,” he added, “and I don’t know there ever will be again.”
Researchers contacted by AFP tended to agree.

By “turning political rallies into entertainment,” Trump “takes alleged negative emotions such as resentment, grievance and disappointment and transforms them into excitement, pride and positive anticipation,” explained Yagmur Karakaya, a sociology professor at Yale University.
He relies on improvised comedy and culture-war jabs, sports metaphors, the ever-present “winning” philosophy, and business jargon, weaving it into a unique style.
“Can others do this? I am not so sure,” Karakaya said.

That is the million-dollar question, said speech communication professor Jacob Justice of the University of Mississippi, who likened a Trump rally’s atmosphere to that of “a Grateful Dead concert (or) a college football tailgate.”
If anyone could inspire something similar, he or she “might come from the world of social media influencing or podcasting,” Justice said.
Should that person be JD Vance, rallygoer Bart said, “he would bring half of these people.” — AFP
40dd9b0c9bd1f9a2: VARGEM GRANDE, Oct 22 — The first time he ate his fill, Walter dos Santos was 25 years old and had long since watched siblings die of hunger in northeastern Brazil, where they grew up without electricity, education, or prospects.
He learned to read and write and finished high school at 32. Today, his daughter holds a doctorate in biotechnology and his son is an agronomist.
The 56-year-old, who lives in Maranhao state, credits one man: Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Dos Santos said Lula was the “father and the mother and the grandfather” of Quilombo Piqui da Rampa—a traditional Afro-Brazilian community descended from enslaved people.
“Everything we were denied, our children can now have,” thanks to Lula’s social policies, he told AFP from his painted yellow house, a far cry from the mud-and-thatch-roofed structure he grew up in.
“Even if people call it handouts, for us they were an enormous help. Because anyone who has ever gone hungry knows not to take these programs for granted.”
His gratitude reflects Lula’s enduring appeal in Brazil’s vast Northeast, where he won nearly 64 percent of votes in a first-round election.
However, he lost over 250,000 votes compared to a 2022 election, which experts say is a sign voters are starting to look beyond social programs to improve their lives.
Nationally, Lula suffered a major blow as right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro defied polls to come out ahead. The pair face a tight runoff on Sunday.
A little ball of rice

Maranhao stretches from the Amazon rainforest to the Atlantic coast, where turquoise lagoons shimmer between the sweeping white dunes of Lencois Maranhenses. Once a major exporter of sugar and cotton, its economy built on enslaved labor, the state is now Brazil’s poorest.

Residents in communities around the city of Vargem Grande told AFP that before Lula first came to power in 2003, theirs was a hardscrabble life of subsistence farming and working in exchange for sugar, tobacco or cachaca (a Brazilian spirit).
“Mom would cook a single kilo of rice to feed everyone. She’d just take a small portion—a little ball of rice—for herself to eat,” said Dos Santos, who was one of 16 children.
Thick groves of babassu palms cover the landscape, for generations providing backbreaking work for women, who crack open the plants’ nuts to extract seeds used to make oil.

Residents of the region credit social programs championed by Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva with reducing poverty and expanding access to education, helping maintain his strong electoral support in Brazil's Northeast ahead of the presidential runoff election. — AFP pic
Maria de Fatima Mendes Ferreira, 54, who lives in the nearby Padre Trindade community, recalls losing her six-month-old baby—one of nine children—to malnutrition in her twenties.
“Back then, we didn’t eat properly. We worked all day long” cracking coconuts.

Her husband, fisherman Antonio Carlos Lima Ferreira, 51, said programs like Lula’s Bolsa Familia—which provides cash to low-income families who keep their children in school and vaccinated—had changed their life.
Lula “has a genuine love for the poor. That’s the crux of it.”
Programs that help locals sell their produce to the government, which in turn uses it to provide school meals and help families in need, have transformed these communities.
Beyond basic necessities
Vitor Hugo Miro, a researcher at the Brazilian Institute of Economics, said the poverty rate—below 775 reais ($154) a month—dropped from 67 percent to 49 percent in Maranhao between 2012 and 2025.
But he said economic opportunity and good jobs are limited, and people are increasingly worried about security as major criminal factions have expanded in the region.
While social programs have been crucial, “people are beginning to weigh other dimensions of their lives when deciding how to vote,” Miro said.

In the regional seaside capital Sao Luis, known for its colonial Portuguese architecture, crumbling tiled facades and cobbled streets, Larissa Bianque, 32, told AFP she was the only one in her family voting for Bolsonaro.
While much of her family depends on Bolsa Familia and other benefits, she said young people “aspire to something beyond just the aid that covers basic necessities.”
Quintessential Northeasterner
For Lula supporters, his life story growing up dirt poor is key to his appeal and gave a sense of pride to a region often mocked as backward and uneducated.
“He is the quintessential Northeasterner... yet he never forgot his roots,” said Zacarias Neto de Moraes, 58, a coordinator with Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT).
He spoke to AFP on the sidelines of a meeting discussing how to deal with a record abstention rate in the region.
“There is a segment of society made up of young people who never lived through the time before Lula. They don’t know what things were like back then,” he said. — AFP
df18d7b7a2f7a11d: JERUSALEM, Oct 22 — When Israel goes to the polls this month, voters will weigh in on military conscription, the economy and how the state should investigate its inability to prevent Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack.
AFP looks at the key issues shaping the campaign as Israel gears up for elections on October 27.
Accountability for October 7
Many Israelis have demanded an independent state commission of inquiry into the failures that allowed Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, which resulted in the deaths of more than 1,200 people.
The deadliest day in Israel’s history, it inflicted a profound national trauma whose repercussions continue to shape the country’s politics, society and collective psyche.

Israel has launched commissions of inquiry after previous national crises, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s main challenger in the upcoming poll, ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot, has pledged to do so again, calling it “a way to prevent the next disaster”.
But Netanyahu’s government, which was in office when the attack occurred, has rejected the calls.
Instead, it has blamed the security establishment for failing to prevent the assault and proposed a bipartisan commission whose members would be appointed by politicians.
Opposition figure Yair Lapid said the government-proposed commission’s purpose “is to whitewash (those responsible) and prevent a genuine investigation”.
Netanyahu himself has faulted the security services for not waking him sooner on the day of the attack.
He faces mounting accusations that he ignored early warnings—notably from the UAE, which reportedly told him Hamas was planning a major operation.

The premier has also come under increased scrutiny over his government’s past dealings with Qatar, which backed Hamas financially with Israeli approval and has long hosted the group’s political leadership.
Future security strategy
For decades, Israel’s security doctrine has rested on three principles: strong intelligence, deterrence and short wars.
But that changed after October 7.
The government has instead embraced long military campaigns, reflected in the army’s continued presence in “security zones” in Gaza, southern Lebanon and Syria.

It also carries out near-daily operations in the occupied West Bank, has launched two wars with Iran and has conducted strikes against Yemen’s Tehran-backed Houthi rebels, fuelling debate over the country’s ability to sustain a military deployed on multiple fronts.
Tens of thousands of reservists have been repeatedly mobilised since 2023, often at significant personal and economic cost, while military leaders continue to warn of manpower shortages.

“We have gone from a logic of deterrence and prosperity between wars to a society that lives permanently by the sword,” said Ofer Shelah, a researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies (INSS).

The campaigns have come at a cost to Israel’s reputation, drawing fierce international criticism, particularly over the war in Gaza, where the Palestinian death toll has exceeded 74,000, according to the territory’s health ministry.

Even US President Donald Trump publicly rebuked Netanyahu over Israel’s conduct during the latest conflict with Iran, at one point launching a profanity-laced tirade after fresh Israeli strikes on Lebanon threatened to derail ceasefire negotiations.
Religion, identity, conscription
With the military facing manpower shortages, the debate over exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews has evolved into a broader argument over Israel’s identity.

Ultra-Orthodox parties want to preserve exemptions that allow religious students to avoid military service, and they are backed by Netanyahu’s Likud party and, by and large, by its far-right coalition partners.
But opposition parties support ending the exemptions and have said they would refuse to join any government that includes ultra-Orthodox parties.
Eisenkot—who lost a son in the Gaza war—has also taken aim at the exemptions, characterising Netanyahu’s government as one that “promotes evasion of duty without shame”.

Netanyahu, meanwhile, has struggled to strike a balance on the issue, recently criticising the arrest of ultra-Orthodox draft dodgers in an interview, while also insisting that those not engaged in full-time Torah study should enlist.
The issue has spawned protests by ultra-Orthodox demonstrators, including one in which they stormed the home of Israel’s military police chief.
But the divide extends beyond military service.

Just days before parliament was dissolved, the outgoing coalition introduced measures promoting gender separation in some public spaces and passed legislation emphasising the importance of Torah study.
Supporters say these policies strengthen Israel’s Jewish character, but critics argue they move the country toward greater religious influence over public life.
Surging cost of living
While security dominates the political debate, the economy remains a major concern for many voters.
Despite strong economic growth, with GDP more than doubling since 2000 and unemployment historically low, Israelis continue to face one of the world’s highest costs of living.
At the same time, median wages remain below the OECD average, putting increasing pressure on households.
Economists point to long-standing structural problems, including housing shortages, trade barriers and limited competition in key sectors, as the main drivers of high prices.
The wars have added another challenge.
Since 2023, Israel’s defence budget has doubled, placing growing pressure on public finances. — AFP
83b67ce293650c2e: MEXICO CITY, Oct 22 — In a workshop in the Mexican town of San Salvador Huixcolotla, three men use small hammers and chisels to punch holes in thick sheets of tissue paper ahead of the Dia de Muertos (Day of the Dead) festival.
The multicolored paper perforated with intricate folk art designs is known as “papel picado” (pecked paper).
It is a central element in the lavish altars erected to the deceased on November 1-2 and is also used to festoon homes and streets.
Papel picado originated in this small central Mexican town in the late 19th century.
More than a century later, three-quarters of the town’s 17,000 inhabitants are employed in producing the paper, which is exported worldwide.
Despite the advent of AI and 3D printing, many people here continue making the paper by hand.

“We get satisfaction from the idea that our craftsmanship is recognized in other countries and that people see value in handmade things,” Miguel Reynoso, a 58-year-old papel picado producer, told AFP.
Reynoso has been in the business for 40 years.
He and his wife employ over a dozen people, including their four daughters, making decorative banners for clients as far away as South Korea and Japan.
The garlands are in demand year-round for events such as baptisms and “quinceaneras” (girls’ 15th birthdays, a major milestone in Latin America).
But orders skyrocket in the lead-up to the Day of the Dead, when hundreds of thousands of sheets of paper are used to deck out towns and cities.
My tradition
The art of making papel picado was born on ranches outside Huixcolotla.
Following a Mesoamerican tradition, farm workers used to etch simple geometric designs into thick paper made from tree bark.
The arrival of fine tissue paper from China in the mid-19th century revolutionized the process, allowing for greater sophistication.
Nowadays, the paper too is manufactured in Huixcolotla, which prides itself on controlling the entire process.
Even the chisels—straight, curved or zigzag, depending on the motif—are made here.
The palette of colors used in the paper has evolved over time to include shades associated with Mexican design, such as lime and Mexican pink (fuchsia).
Roberto Carlos carefully carves a skull adorned with an elegant hat into a wad of deep purple paper 50 sheets deep.
If the paper tears, he has to discard the lot, which is why you have to “be very delicate,” the 34-year-old artisan explained.
Mari Reynoso, Miguel’s 26-year-old daughter, acknowledged that “industrialization” threatened her town’s bread and butter.
The disappearance of handicrafts, “a symbol of Mexico,” would be a blow to the country’s heritage, she argued.
“Just seeing them makes people say: ‘This is culture, this is my tradition.’” — AFP
156eb47b23d11f0b: SANTIAGO, Oct 22 — The world is hungrier than ever for copper, a key ingredient in green energy and the data centres that power artificial intelligence.
But Chile, which accounts for one-quarter of the world’s supply of the critical mineral, has seen its output of its biggest export fall in recent years.
In August, production fell to its lowest level in 15 years, even though strong global demand is keeping prices buoyant.
Why is output falling?
Chile’s woes are largely due to the age of its mines.
After decades of extraction, the biggest deposits have been depleted, meaning companies have to process ever more ore to obtain the same quantities of the metal.

“You have to invest more money, undertake much greater maintenance efforts, and that also means more demanding technical requirements,” Juan Carlos Guajardo, founder of the Chilean consultancy Plusmining, told AFP.
To offset the drop in productivity, mining companies have moved to expand and modernize their mines.
But several projects suffered delays, cost overruns or technical problems, Nicolas Munoz, an analyst at London-based consultancy CRU Group, noted.
State-owned Codelco was, for example, forced to suspend expansion of the El Teniente mine – Chile’s largest – after studies flagged up seismic risks.
Meanwhile, mines in northern and central Chile were forced to reduce operations in July and August due to heavy rains linked to El Nino that knocked out power and hampered access to the sites.
These setbacks come a year after Codelco’s largest mine, El Teniente, was forced to suspend part of its production for months following an accident that left six workers dead.
How have markets reacted?
The drop in Chile’s output has put pressure on global supplies, causing prices to hit a record US$14,875 (RM60,700) a ton in September.
A further unexpected decline in production could force importers to look for alternative suppliers, according to Munoz.
The International Energy Agency anticipates a 25-per cent copper supply deficit by 2035 if new deposits are not developed worldwide.
Copper’s biggest clients are worried that Chile “does not have a significant production-increase pipeline in sight,” said Guajardo.
“That means the rest of the world will have to make a greater effort (to make up the shortfall).”
Chile’s market share has fallen from 34 per cent in 2010 to around 23 per cent today, according to the US Geological Survey.
The decline is hitting the economy. Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz said this month that it had knocked “at least one percentage point” off GDP this year.
How can Chile rebound?
There is no quick fix, according to Guajardo and Munoz, who argue that Chile must restore production at its biggest mines and move forward with expansion and modernization projects.
In the longer term, they say, the country needs to develop new deposits.
“It’s not an issue that can be solved with a law or a regulatory change. It’s a systematic effort that has to be undertaken,” said Guajardo.
Munoz highlights the need to streamline mining permits, attract investment and improve infrastructure, especially in energy, logistics and water, which the industry requires.
CRU consultancy nevertheless forecasts output of around 5.5 million tons of copper in 2027, up from the 5.27 million tons projected by the Chilean Copper Commission for this year.
The medium-term outlook is more positive, with CRU forecasting up to 6 million tons by 2030 as new projects come online. — AFP
cbfe464dc8e8e45f: Attackers are hammering servers with millions of attempts to exploit the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, with Amazon revealing that someone was already going after the flaws four days before they were publicly disclosed.
Cloudflare says it has recorded a staggering increase in attacks targeting the two vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, since details began circulating earlier this week.

According to Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince, the company spotted thousands of exploitation attempts in the 10 hours before the vulnerabilities were publicly announced. That figure jumped to tens of thousands within 45 minutes of disclosure, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and has since climbed into the millions.

And the attackers aren't simply recycling the same exploit. Cloudflare said it has seen miscreants tweaking their payloads in an attempt to sneak past its web application firewall (WAF) protections, apparently using feedback from blocked requests to work out what might get through.
Security outfit Hadrian also sounded the alarm on October 21, reporting that PHP2Shell was being "exploited in the wild at scale."
"Most of the attacks we observe abuse PHP's session upload-progress path, and we expect more exploit paths to appear before and after the fix ships," the company warned.
More worrying, some attackers appear to have started before the vulnerabilities were even public knowledge.

Amazon Threat Intelligence says it detected an attempt to exploit PHP2Shell on October 17, four days before patches were released. The activity was picked up by MadPot, Amazon's network of honeypots designed to lure attackers and record what they get up to.

"While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure," Amazon said.

The retail and cloud giant said it detected multiple proof-of-concept exploits on October 21, with the earliest appearing around 0200 UTC, some 12 hours before the patches were released. Over the following six hours, further attempts arrived from different anonymized infrastructure, using a variety of payloads. Amazon reckons this points to multiple attackers rather than a single group.
Whether any of those attempts would have worked against real-world systems remains unclear.

The findings add another layer to an already messy disclosure. As The Register reported on Wednesday, the PHP Foundation has accused supply-chain security vendor Chainguard of putting websites at risk by publishing patched PHP builds before the agreed disclosure deadline.
However, Amazon's October 17 detection suggests at least one cybercrim was already trying to exploit the bugs days before that incident.

The vulnerabilities themselves are particularly nasty. Both carry a critical 9.2 severity rating and affect PHP's handling of memory, potentially allowing unauthenticated attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers.

Unlike flaws in individual plugins or applications, these bugs affect the PHP runtime itself, putting a potentially enormous number of websites at risk regardless of which content management system they use.
Cloudflare says it has deployed WAF protections across its free and paid plans, although it has stressed that these are no substitute for patching.

With attackers already trying their luck before the fixes were available, admins may have more than just a patching backlog to worry about. Amazon is advising organizations to investigate suspicious activity dating back to at least October 17, rather than assuming their systems were safe until the vulnerabilities became public. ®

6fcd064ec64e90f5: China-aligned attackers used AI agents and compromised ConnectWise application credentials to target more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, Microsoft says.

The Windows giant revealed this week that the attackers, tracked as Storm-0940, used an open source AI penetration-testing tool called ARTEX to automate attacks against Microsoft 365 environments. In some cases, they went from picking a target to gaining privileged cloud access in less than three hours.

The findings shed more light on the ConnectWise security incident, which saw the IT management vendor pull the plug on its Cloud Backup, SaaS Security, and Cloud Management services after discovering unauthorized access to application identities.
ConnectWise didn't initially identify who was responsible, but Microsoft has now pointed the finger at Storm-0940, a China-linked espionage crew that's been operating since at least 2021.
The group has traditionally relied on the usual tricks, including password spraying and exploiting internet-facing applications, but this time it used AI to do some of the heavy lifting.

ARTEX is an open source penetration-testing framework written in Go that uses AI agents to automate everything from reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery to credential attacks and data theft. Microsoft says Storm-0940 began using it as early as September to target organizations worldwide, including government agencies, defense contractors, banks, manufacturers, and tech firms.

Between October 10 and 14, the hackers made more than 151,000 failed sign-in attempts against 327 accounts at eight organizations. Microsoft observed no successful logins from that password-spraying campaign, but then the attackers shifted to compromised ConnectWise application identities.
The compromised application credentials let the attackers exploit permissions customers had already granted to ConnectWise services, without needing an interactive user login.

Armed with ARTEX, Storm-0940 attempted to authenticate against more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, at times reaching 2,900 attempts a minute. Microsoft also observed AI-accelerated activity through Microsoft Graph, including reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges, potentially allowing the attackers to stick around even after the original credentials were revoked.

Most attempts failed, though Microsoft says the hackers still managed to establish persistent privileged access at numerous organizations. It hasn't disclosed how many customers were compromised or whether any data was stolen, cautioning that a successful login doesn't necessarily mean information was accessed.

ConnectWise CEO Manny Rivelo said the company had contained the affected application connections and was gradually restoring services, although shutting down those connections wouldn't necessarily boot out attackers who had already established a foothold in customer environments.

ConnectWise has been here before. In May 2025, it admitted that a "sophisticated nation-state actor" had broken into its systems and compromised a small number of customers using its ScreenConnect remote access software. There's nothing to suggest the two attacks are linked.
Nor is Storm-0940 alone in making use of ARTEX. Microsoft says it has spotted attackers from several geographic regions using the framework, which is freely available for penetration testing.

The underlying techniques are nothing new – stolen credentials, password spraying, and application abuse – but Microsoft says AI helped Storm-0940 execute them faster, with some attacks progressing from initial targeting to privileged cloud access in under three hours. ®

7a5dff398a4c13fb: In 2015, all but two countries agreed to make an effort to keep global temperatures from reaching 1.5° C above pre-industrial readings. Since then, most of the world has largely treated what they signed on to as aspirational, and one of the largest emitters (the US) has alternately withdrawn and recommitted to the agreement. Meanwhile, the planet has responded as expected to steadily rising carbon emissions and appears to be practically at the 1.5° limit.

On Wednesday, for the first time, the United Nations Environmental Programme (UNEP) acknowledged that reality and conceded that the goal of keeping warming below 1.5° was no longer a viable one. Instead, its new goalposts focus on keeping both how long we exceed that limit and how much we exceed it by, at a minimum. Doing that will require both dramatic emissions cuts now and the removal of hundreds of gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere before the century is out.

Depending on which baseline you use to establish pre-industrial temperatures, as well as which reconstruction of global temperatures you rely on, the world has either gotten very close to, or already exceeded, the 1.5° milestone. The current El Niño event, which appears exceptionally strong, will almost certainly mean that we've gone over it no matter which records you choose.

4dbbc2953d2974b4: Japan's mission to the Martian moon Phobos launched this week, with a veteran European probe expected to be waiting when it arrives.

JAXA, Japan's space agency, confirmed that the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft launched aboard an H3 rocket on October 19 at 19:41 UTC – October 20 in Japan. On October 21, it said that initial critical operations, including solar array deployment, were complete. Equipment checks will follow as the spacecraft prepares for its outbound cruise.

The probe is due to reach Mars in 2027, deploy the Idefix rover on Phobos, and attempt one or two landings on the moon itself. The rover is named after the dog from the Asterix comics. Scientists plan to collect about 10 g of material from Phobos and send it to Earth, with a return planned for 2031.

The European Space Agency (ESA) is supporting the trip with Mars Express (MEX), which has orbited Mars since 2003. A former team member told The Register that plans include joint observations and imaging of MMX's landing site.

MEX's latest mission extension runs to 2029, covering MMX's expected arrival. The former team member described it as definitely the last – before adding that "the first 'last ever extension' was in about 2007."

Discussions about another "last ever extension" could begin in 2028 or 2029, with support for MMX and the Rosalind Franklin rover among the potential reasons to keep MEX going. Funding and scientific returns would determine the outcome. A software update announced in May 2025 reduced wear on its gyroscopes, potentially allowing them to last until 2034.

Rosalind Franklin is due for launch in 2028 after repeated delays and Russia's ejection from the project. MEX will likely be able to image the rover's landing site on the surface of Mars and take part in data relay operations, though ESA's Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) will be the main relay asset.

Several years ago, another team member joked that MEX was so tough it would punch straight through Phobos if sent there for disposal. We wouldn't take that as an engineering assessment, but it says something about the team's affection for their spacecraft.

MEX's longevity is a tribute to its builders and operators. With funding through 2029, it could welcome MMX next year. Further extensions might keep it working through the sample-return departure and Rosalind Franklin's arrival.
"We all want our '30 years in flight' T-shirts," the former team member said. ®

00bb17bb6751ebb5: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 22 — Two men who went viral on social media after crashing into public vehicles while attempting to evade police in Bukit Antarabangsa were charged in three separate courts in Ampang today on various offences, including obstructing civil servants, possessing dangerous weapons and drugs.

47f9432a28fb5645: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 22 — The Court of Appeal today overturned a High Court decision that had released a wheelchair-bound man on bail pending the disposal of his drug trafficking trial.

A three-man bench led by Justice Datuk Choo Kah Sing, alongside K. Muniandy and Datuk Seri Latifah Mohd Tahar, allowed the prosecution’s appeal to set aside the High Court’s ruling and ordered M. Alagesan to be remanded in custody.
Justice Choo, who delivered the unanimous decision, however, granted the defence’s application for Alagesan to be placed at the Sungai Buloh Hospital until the conclusion of his trial.
He held that the High Court judge erred in applying Section 388 of the Criminal Procedure Code to allow bail when there is an express law dealing with bail for drug trafficking offences.

He said the High Court’s decision was against the provision of Section 41B (1) (a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act, which states that bail shall not be granted to an accused person charged under the Act with an offence punishable by death or life imprisonment with not less than 12 strokes of the cane.
Justice Choo said Section 2 of the same Act stated that this subsection shall have the effect notwithstanding any written laws or any rule of law to the contrary.
The court ordered the RM150,000 bail deposited to be returned and revoked all previously imposed bail conditions.
“This court ordered the trial court to fix an early hearing date to complete the trial by the end of this year if possible considering the health condition of the accused,” Justice Choo said.

Earlier, lawyer Datuk Naran Singh, assisted by Amrick Singh Sandu, told the court that the trial dates have been scheduled for Feb 17 to 19 and March 24 to 26, 2027, and requested the court to issue a directive for the trial to be heard earlier.
Alagesan, 44, was charged with trafficking in 6.276 kg of cannabis at a house in Kg KL Tin Kalumpang, Kuala Kubu Baru, Hulu Selangor, Selangor on Feb 7, 2024.

On Sept 23, 2024, the Shah Alam High Court allowed Alagesan’s application to be released on bail pending disposal of his trial with RM150,000 with two sureties and imposed additional conditions including reporting to the nearest police station, surrendering his passport, and remaining at home from 7 pm to 7 am.

During proceedings, deputy public prosecutor Hafizah Johor Ariff Johor argued that Section 41B(1)(a) establishes a mandatory restriction that completely denies the right to bail for offences carrying the death penalty under the Dangerous Drugs Act, thereby divesting the High Court of any discretionary power to release the accused on bail pending completion of the trial.

She said that the High Court’s decision to grant bail in this case is a departure from established legal principles and it would open the door for thousands of detainees facing charges under Section 39B of the Dangerous Drug Act to apply for bail on subjective health grounds, thereby crippling Parliament’s intention to combat serious drug crimes.
In response, Naran Singh contended that despite the statutory prohibition under Section 41B, the court retains the inherent power to grant bail under exceptional circumstances.
He said Alagesan was paralysed from the waist down and was unable to squat, noting that standard prison toilets are equipped with squatting facilities. — Bernama
