dc2ecfeed8750825: From Moaz Nair

The persistent, fractured politicking among Indian political leaders has devolved into a tragic spectacle of self-preservation, birthing a swarm of toothless, ego-driven factions that have completely abandoned the community’s most vulnerable.
For decades, these leaders have traded genuine community advancement for personal clout and minor cabinet crumbs, leaving working-class Indians politically homeless.

Ironically, as the Indian demographic footprint shrinks, the number of these redundant, self-serving political groups keeps multiplying — each shouting from its own small hill while achieving absolutely nothing of substance.

If these career politicians truly possess an ounce of genuine care for the marginalised, they must immediately halt their petty bickering, dismantle their hollow factions, and focus on delivering institutional, non-negotiable economic welfare.

Recent demographic data from the statistics department covering 2016 to 2026 lays bare a damning reality. In just one decade, the Indian component of the citizen population shrivelled from 7% to 6.5%. Representing roughly 5.8% of the total national population, ethnic Indians total about 2.1 million citizens.
Behind these dwindling percentages lies an unsettling truth: a minority community is fast becoming adrift from the mainstream of national development.

Approximately 38.7% of the community falls into the Bottom 40% (B40) income bracket, translating to 227,000 households. More alarming still, the data indicates that 10% of these B40 families — around 22,000 households — survive on less than RM2,000 a month in extreme precarity.
However, a shrinking population footprint must never be used as a political excuse for a diminished national commitment.

Instead, this demographic decline demands an immediate paradigm shift — shattering the status quo of lazy, generic handouts and replacing them with high-impact policy interventions built upon three non-negotiable pillars.
The 2027 budget attempts to tackle these imbalances, but its success will hinge on execution.
Equity, asset ownership, and economic empowerment

A shrinking population share inherently dilutes purchasing power and locks minority communities out of wealth accumulation. To bridge this widening wealth chasm, outdated asset ownership policies must be aggressively dismantled.
This means enforcing strict, mandatory quotas and dedicated housing funds to guarantee B40 Indian households affordable housing.
The 2027 budget confronts these capital deficits by channelling a combined RM150 million through Tekun Nasional and Amanah Ikhtiar Malaysia.

This includes a dedicated RM100 million Indian Community Entrepreneur Development Scheme to provide critical capital to small business owners, and RM50 million in microcredit loans customised to uplift Indian women entrepreneurs.
Ensuring families own homes and hold financial assets is vital to systematically engineering sustainable, multi-generational social mobility.
TVET overhaul and educational infrastructure

A radical technical and vocational education and training (TVET) overhaul and digital empowerment must disrupt a stagnant workforce. The brutal job market of tomorrow will show no mercy to obsolete skillsets.
Indian youth — particularly those trapped in forgotten suburban fringes and estates — must be aggressively channelled into high-tier TVET ecosystems.

The 2027 budget offers a vital fiscal upgrade here. The allocation for the Malaysian Indian Transformation Unit (Mitra) has been boosted to RM150 million, specifically earmarked to help youths make the transition into high-skilled industrial pipelines. Furthermore, Indian youth must tap into the wider national RM8 billion TVET budget.

Equally foundational is confronting the historical deficits in education infrastructure. Malaysia’s 528 Tamil national-type primary schools (SJKT) carry a complex legacy, with 324 operating as government-assisted institutions sitting on private estate or community trust lands.

This has historically locked many schools out of direct development funding, leaving 68% of them without basic ICT laboratories. The 2027 budget addresses this digital divide with a RM50 million allocation for essential repairs, rewiring, and basic amenities, alongside full reconstruction priorities for severe emergencies like at SJKT Dengkil in Selangor and SJKT Gopeng in Perak.
Ruthless structural reform for targeted poverty alleviation
The survival of these policies hinges entirely on a ruthless structural reform of Mitra. For decades, fragmented agendas and redundant aid distribution have sabotaged state interventions.

Mitra must be stripped of bureaucracy and given absolute, transparent, and centralised power over data, funding, and execution. Armed with a unified database, cost-of-living aid, scholarships, and micro-business grants can finally bypass bureaucratic gridlock.

Crucially, the ultimate success of the budget for working-class Indians relies on broader macroeconomic shifts. The mandated minimum wage hike to RM2,000 per month starting June 2027 will immediately lift the community’s most vulnerable 22,000 households out of deep financial distress, especially when combined with the RM16 billion Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah cash aid pool.
Moving beyond salvation

Ultimately, the integrity of Malaysia’s future will be judged by how it treats its most vulnerable. Addressing this demographic collapse is not a bloodless numbers game on a spreadsheet; it is an urgent battle for socioeconomic justice.
By executing these progressive policy pillars, the country can transform a demographic challenge into a powerful reservoir of human capital.

However, relying solely on external political salvation is a failing strategy. If the Indian community is to survive as a relevant economic force in Malaysia’s shifting landscape, it must aggressively dismantle internal fatalism.

Upward mobility cannot be granted by policy alone. Real transformation demands that the community fiercely engineer its own self-upliftment — taking absolute ownership of its wealth, its trajectory, and its future generations.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

8215ef4d36d93f56: Nvidia has decided that its future prospects rest on an improved silicon substrate and packing supply chain, so has dipped into its giant pile of cash to ensure it can get the parts it needs by ensuring its suppliers have the resources needed to play their small part in keeping the flow of GPUs and AI processors strong.

It’s not unusual for manufacturers to invest in their suppliers, because it helps to create certainty and spread financial risk. For those deals to be announced at a major tech company’s conference – as Nvidia did at its Berlin GTC gabfest – is somewhat novel, suggesting the company feels the need to show investors it is working to ensure it can meet demand for its products, and that demand will persist for years.

Several of Nvidia’s announcements pertained to silicon substrates, aka wafers. Whatever you call them, they’re blank, round, silicon slabs onto which chipmakers etch circuits. They’re made by companies that sell to foundries like TSMC and Intel, which then turn them into chips of various flavours.
At GTC Berlin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang observed that demand for AI hardware is vast, but that “Capacity is the constraint.”
Specifically, capacity for activities like building substrates, advanced silicon packaging, testing, and creating optical connectors.
Big Green therefore plans to increase substrate capacity for its products by 2.5x over the next three years.

To make that happen, Nvidia has added Samsung’s Electro-Mechanics business unit to its substrate supply chain. Samsung apparently has immediate capacity at a factory in South Korea and Nvidia intends to tap that now. The deal means that by 2028, about a quarter of Sammy’s substrate output will go to Nvidia.
Nvidia already has a deal with Japanese substrate outfit IBIDEN. In Berlin, the GPU giant pointed to further expansion that will triple production at an IBIDEN plant.
Taiwanese substrate player Unimicron is also benefiting from Nvidia’s generosity, in the form of a capacity reservation agreement and associated plant expansion plans.

It’s not just wafers that Nvidia wants to tuck into. The company has also signed a capacity reservation with Korean silicon packaging player Amkor. Again, Big Green’s involvement will see its partner expand capacity, in this case by 300 percent.
Nvidia says this deal “will support higher production volumes for current and next-generation platforms.”

AI systems need speedy networks, and many players see optical connections as the best way to build systems capable of handling the data deluges modern workloads create and require. Nvidia has therefore hatched a plan to boost manufacturing capacity at optics outfit SPIL. Again, Big Green already has a deal with the company, but in Berlin it expanded that arrangement in the hope it expands production capacity 15x by mid-2027, then doubles that again by the end of 2028.
All of which suggests that Nvidia believes the AI infrastructure boom has years left to run. ®

e3f519129b2e62b1: Whenever a minimum wage announcement falls short of public expectations, the political knee-jerk reaction is to aim all arrows at Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.
Yet, directing the blame solely at him misses the real dynamics behind Malaysia’s wage policy formulation.

First, consider how policy recommendations are shaped. Talent Corp and the human resources ministry paid RM1 million to a consulting firm specifically to research and recommend an appropriate minimum wage rate.
When the government relies on external subject-matter experts, paid handsomely with public funds, it acts on structured economic assessments rather than arbitrary political whims.
If the resulting figure feels inadequate to the working public, we must scrutinise the methodology, data and assumptions used by these highly paid consultants first.
The research, findings, and identity of these consultants ought to be made public for full transparency and proper scrutiny before rushing to condemn the prime minister.

Second, the relentless pushback from employer groups continues to stall wage growth. Business associations and industry groups routinely lobby against wage increases, warning of economic ruin and mass layoffs.

Their aggressive pushback invariably leads to exemptions and now deferred compliance for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), diluting the impact of wage reforms across major sectors of the economy.
Meanwhile, Anwar’s track record demonstrates a consistent commitment to raising worker compensation.
The minimum wage has risen 33% under the Madani government from RM1,500 in 2022 to RM2,000 in 2027. Graduates and semi-skilled workers will have a new minimum monthly salary of RM2,500.

Under Anwar’s administration, government-linked companies (GLCs) have actively led by example, setting a baseline living wage that was raised in Budget 2027 from RM3,100 to RM3,400. This upward revision reflects a genuine drive to ensure decent standards of living where the government holds direct leverage.

The true obstacles to a higher floor wage are not found in the prime minister’s office. The real villains in this story are the corporate lobbies constantly fighting wage increases and the consultants who produce conservative recommendations despite million-ringgit fees.

Rather than make Anwar the scapegoat, public discourse should demand accountability from the consultants who drafted the proposal and the employer groups who consistently undermine fair pay for Malaysian workers.

That said, according to research and analysis published in The Economist, governments should be cautious about aggressive minimum wage hikes due to mounting evidence of hidden economic distortions and better alternative policy tools.

Research from Nobel Prize winner David Card and others in the 1990s showed that the negative impact of minimum wages was overstated and job-losses were offset by higher spending and economic activity.

Recent studies, such as evaluations of sharp minimum wage increases in places like Seattle, show that high-wage floors can slow down the hiring of low-wage workers and reduce total work hours rather than cause immediate mass layoffs.
To offset higher baseline pay, employers often resort to unpredictable scheduling, fewer workplace perks, or higher output demands that can lead to increased workplace accidents.
High minimum wages are a blunt tool for fighting poverty because many minimum-wage earners live in households with high-earning family members.
Businesses, especially in labour-intensive or low-margin sectors, frequently pass higher wage costs onto consumers through rising prices, triggering affordability pressures.

The Economist highlights alternatives such as in-work tax credits, the progressive wage policy (PWP) in Malaysia or reverse income taxes, as superior approaches because they target low-income households directly without creating the same economic distortions or hidden costs.
Regular readers of this column will be familiar with these ideas because I have advocated them for many years and they have recently been adopted by Bersama.

a0c83e482733c7fa: PHP developers have accused software supply chain security shop Chainguard of effectively revealing critical bugs in the open-source scripting language ahead of a planned official disclosure.
On Wednesday, just hours after releasing emergency patches for the two bugs collectively called PHP2shell, PHP maintainers published a blog about how the vulnerabilities were found and fixed.

They credited researchers at Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz with finding the security holes between August and September. All three companies have said they used AI models to find the vulnerabilities, which are now tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on servers running PHP.

This is especially serious because PHP powers huge chunks of the public web. It also adds a dose of irony to the “leak and disrupted disclosure” part of the blog, which blames Chainguard - a company that aims to secure software supply chains by hardening open source code - for the messy disclosure.

The trouble, according to PHP developers, started on Tuesday around 15:00 UTC, when “two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media,” along with incorrect information about the release time and CVSS severity rating. At that point, no technical details leaked.
The rumors, however, prompted PHP maintainers to warn people in advance about the critical flaws, and move the planned disclosure forward a day, from Thursday to Wednesday.

“Distributors were still packaging the fix, so releasing immediately would have left many users without an easy way to update,” the PHP Foundation blog says. “Moving the release forward by one day was the best compromise between acting quickly, giving people time to prepare, and making sure everyone had a simple update path when the vulnerabilities were disclosed.”
A couple of hours later, Calif “mistakenly” published a video showing a proof-of-concept exploit and “additional, though limited” information about the bugs, we’re told.

“Mitigation advice we started providing to a few critical infrastructure providers around Oct 20th 23:00 UTC, may have leaked as well,” the PHP blog says, but it does not name these providers. And then it throws Chainguard under the bus:

“On October 21st at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the coordinated release, Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix. Like other distributors, Chainguard had received the patch in advance so its users could update the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed. Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure.”
Chainguard CEO: 'We made the call'
Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc spoke with The Register on Wednesday, and while he doesn’t dispute the timeline, said his company "didn't leak."
“These things are messy,” Lorenc said.

Chainguard learned “something was coming in PHP” on Friday from one of the researchers that found the bugs, Lorenc told us. Later that night, using his company’s AI harness and a frontier model, the CEO and the Chainguard team independently found the same memory corruption vulnerabilities.
All it took was a “basic prompt of ‘find bad vulnerabilities in PHP,’” Lorenc wrote in a subsequent LinkedIn post.
On Saturday, Chainguard began working with the PHP maintainers, confirmed that some of its findings matched the bug reports, and helped test the patches.

“The patches are crazy - this is not a simple vulnerability,” Lorenc told The Register. “It really did take them months to build a real, working patch for it. And then on Monday, the rumors started, and yesterday it just spiraled.”

Some people published POCs on social media, other security vendors reported seeing real-world exploitation, and late Tuesday night Lorenc told us he decided to ship the fixes, and notified the PHP coordinated disclosure channel about his plans.

“People were getting hit in advance” of the official PHP disclosure, “so we made the call to ship the fixes under that,” Lorenc said. “It's coordinated vulnerability disclosure, unless there's evidence of active exploits in the wild.”
Also on Tuesday night, Chainguard published built artifacts and made them accessible to anyone, not just customers. “And then I woke up this morning and saw that this was all our fault,” Lorenc said.

When asked if he would do anything differently, given the fallout from Chainguard’s early disclosure, Lorenc said no. “This process and policy is based on trying to coordinate as much as possible until shit hits the fan and people start weaponizing things,” he said. “It sucks, because we really are all on one team, and there's bad guys over there doing stuff.”
Chainguard’s honeypots trapped IPs from China and Russia targeting the vulnerabilities on Wednesday, Lorenc added.
“Just being told there's a vulnerability in a piece of software - even something as big as PHP - is enough to find it,” he told us. “I did that myself without any other knowledge on Friday."
"I think this is kind of the new normal. People are able to build an exploit in hours without even knowing what the vulnerability is."
What we know about the CVEs and how to exploit them
While we still don’t know the scope of exploitation - or what will happen to vulnerable legacy systems that don’t have security fixes - threat hunters predict it’s going to be a doozy.

“Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them,” Wiz researchers Sagi Tzadik, Shir Tamari, Nir Ohfeld, and Tomer Schwartz warned on Wednesday, adding the oft-quoted stat that PHP powers 70 percent of all websites in the world.

“Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4,” the Wiz kids wrote. “Attackers can exploit them remotely, in some cases fairly easily. Immediate patching is strongly advised.”

Both bugs are related to how PHP handles memory management and error handling, and both lead to remote code execution (RCE). They can cause a corrupted internal PHP state when a request ends unexpectedly, and then a later request can reuse that state, leading to memory disclosure or RCE.

“Both are memory corruption vulnerabilities,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity explained. “If an attacker can shape the memory PHP trusts, they can potentially hijack what it does next, and in these cases that means remote code execution.”

CVE-2026-109618 (GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w) leads to RCE via out-of-memory corruption. “If a request reached PHP's memory_limit at exactly the wrong moment, PHP could leave partially initialized internal data behind and later treat it as valid, corrupting memory,” the project maintainer wrote. “On Apache with mod_php, an unauthenticated request can trigger this before any application code runs.”

CVE-2026-109619 (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp) allows RCE via stale state. “A fatal error at the wrong point could leave internal state pointing to memory that belonged to a previous request,” according to the PGP Foundation. “A later request handled by the same worker could then use that freed memory. A use-after-free and worker crash were confirmed, and the reporter demonstrated remote code execution against a real-world application running on Apache with mod_php.”®

984ee75e2d30573b: Tesla published its third-quarter 2026 financial results this afternoon. Earlier in October, it reported its sales and deliveries for the three-month period, selling fewer cars than in the same quarter in 2025, yet it still beat analyst projections. Now we can see how those sales translate to the bottom line. Tesla brought in $28 billion in revenue in Q3, almost the same as in 2025.

Automotive revenues were $20.6 billion, a 3 percent decrease year over year. Perhaps more troubling is the decline in revenue from solar panels and storage batteries—this line of business had been growing, but for Q3 revenue fell 16 percent year over year to $2.9 billion. Services and other revenues, though, which include parts and Supercharger use, grew by a third to $4.6 billion.

But the company—like the rest of us—has seen its expenses go up. Operating expenses rose by 39 percent to $4.8 billion, dropping the company’s operating margin to just 2.6 percent; in Q3 2025, Tesla’s margin was 5.8 percent. Net profit fell to $787 million, down 43 percent year over year. What’s more, capital expenditures were up by 110 percent to $4.7 billion, and free cash flow was down 62 percent to $1.5 billion.

Knecht previously observed that Steinberger has acknowledged having "a virtually unlimited token budget, which not all of us in the room have."
Responding to the audible surprise rising from the audience, Steinberger added, "What people don't always understand is not all of that is useful."
That only amplified the murmuring, perhaps not the effect he had been after. Meanwhile, his employer, OpenAI, is reportedly trying to "accelerate funding" ahead of rival Anthropic's expected IPO.
Steinberger's subsequent musing about his preferred way of working failed to recognize Knecht's acknowledgement of financial limitations.

"I feel like the main challenge a lot of people still have is that our infrastructure structure hasn't really caught up yet," Steinberger said. "Like why is this still using my computer? Shouldn't this all be in the cloud?"

Apart from the privacy and compliance implications of relying on cloud-based AI, cost remains a consideration for anyone not setting venture funds alight. Cloud-hosted agents can be expensive. Shouldn't this all run locally?

Pointing to the OpenClaw project and how a lot of open source maintainers have given up accepting pull requests due to frustration with AI slop, Knecht asked Steinberger whether we're approaching the death of open source or a golden age of AI.
Steinberger said he thinks the way pull requests are handled needs to change because people don't explain how they arrived at their proposed changed code.
"If I see your thoughts, how you got from A to B, my trust in the output is way higher than if you just throw the finished work across the fence," he said.
Knecht also asked Steinberger whether everyone in the room would have hundreds of AI agents running in a few years.
Steinberger doubts it will be hundreds.

"I think everyone will have some sort of intelligence that runs and thinks and helps them throughout the day or even predicts what could help you in the future," he said. "So instead of asking the question, maybe you already get the answer."
Toward the end of the session, Knecht raised the issue of trust and how to know what data to give to an agent.

That's a hard question, Steinberger admitted. Part of it, he said, has to do with how much you trust the underlying model itself, because so much of model behavior is not governed by the harness – the code that wraps the model.
"A lot of decisions that I built into OpenClaw early on now can change because the models are so much better," he said.
Even if risks like prompt injection have been reduced through engineering efforts, Steinberger said, "you might not want to give your agent all the permissions."
Instead, he suggested using an agent to authorize your agent.

"You want to have another agent that can give it permissions or not and then this agent has to negotiate with another agent," he said. "Many times the agents are like, 'oh yeah, actually maybe I shouldn't do this,' or 'there's a simpler way that keeps it within the guardrails.' So those those two systems combined greatly increase my trust that I just can let the agent rip." ®

05c8eb78562a8d38: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
Introducing: the Impossible issue

We wanted our last print edition of 2026 to include a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s fun to dream about living on other planets or uploading our brains. But also because scientists and engineers who won’t give up on daring endeavors remind us what technology is supposed to do: make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful.

That’s the ambition behind the stories in our new Impossible issue. We explore bold attempts to make synthetic blood, build cities on the moon, and attain cognitive immortality. We investigate AI’s ability to say no, a bionic eye that can restore sight, and high hopes for blended meat. Plus, we check in on six technologies that have been “coming soon” for years.
This issue is for the folks with the audacity to try, and refuse to let anyone—themselves included— tell them no. We hope you enjoy the ride.
Astrolab’s upcoming rover will run the first LLMs on the moon

Large language models are set to go lunar. A computer capable of running AI software is one of the payloads aboard Astrolab’s FLIP lunar rover, which is slated to head to the moon as early as next month.

The mission will test whether LLMs can enable greater autonomy and real-time intelligent decision-making in the extreme lunar environment. But the moon will present formidable challenges, from extreme temperatures to intense cosmic radiation.
Find out how the lunar rover could change the future of space exploration.
—Tereza Pultarova
How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster

In Alaska’s Denali National Park, a 2013 lightning fire burned nearly 35,000 acres, stripping away the insulating layer that preserves permafrost. It’s given scientists a rare opportunity to study how fires reshape permafrost and carbon storage over time.

The work is providing critical clues into the complex mechanisms driving cascading climate feedback effects. As warming temperatures fuel fires, more permafrost thaws, releasing greenhouse-gas emissions that threaten to fuel more warming, fires and permafrost loss. Their observations are revealing worrisome signs about what lies ahead.
Discover what their fieldwork is revealing about a cascading climate disaster.
—James Temple
MIT Technology Review Narrated: the explosive claim that’s upended the AI world

“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the industry on its head.
Cammarata claims that LLMs might be far easier to understand, and thus to monitor and control, than people previously thought. If true, it’s a huge deal. But not everyone is convinced.

MIT Technology Review spoke to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He explained what he thinks researchers are getting wrong, what his work actually shows, and why skeptics aren’t ready to celebrate just yet.

This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

5b3ce3d240be4172: I’d wager everyone has a rehearsed response to what’s absolutely one of the world’s worst interview questions: “What’s your biggest weakness?” Whenever I’ve gotten it, I take a slow—even pensive—breath and rattle off my line: “I say no to myself too much.”

I won’t lie. It’s a bit shameless—a definite humblebrag. I’m a systems thinker: When an idea pops up, I immediately spin up a feasibility assessment in my head. I run lists, plot timelines, and tally budget line items. Sometimes a rough Gantt chart starts to take shape. (I’m a gas at parties, as you can surely tell.)

My brain, throughout my 20-plus-year career as a science and tech journalist, has played host to a near ­constant tug-of-war between ambition and reality. Learning to find that balance is a big part of what’s helped me survive in this industry and, ultimately, led me here. This past spring, I had the great privilege of joining the incredible team of journalists behind MIT Technology Review to take the reins of the print magazine.

If you’ve been reading along with us for the last handful of issues, you may have noticed a few changes starting to materialize. We’ve brought back a regular roster of lists and infographics (both things that magazines do particularly well). But the biggest change is only just beginning to take shape, which is why Mat Honan, our editor in chief, asked me to hop in to introduce myself—and the issue you’re holding in your hands right now.
We’re giving ourselves permission to play around and experiment. To be a little … audacious.

Because, practical though I may be, I do still have plenty of ideas. It’s just that I sometimes need a reminder to stop blocking myself and do the thing. That’s the spirit driving this issue in particular.

We wanted to end 2026 with a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s frankly a lot of fun to dream about living on the moon or uploading our brains. Because losing sight of ambition is all too easy when it feels as if we’re playing whack-a-mole with the world’s problems. But also because the scientists and engineers who absolutely refuse to give up on even the most daring endeavors—like making synthetic blood or decoding animals’ speech—remind us what this whole technology thing is supposed to do to begin with.

It’s supposed to take cutting-edge research and development and apply it to make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful. And when we eff up and make things worse (see: forever chemicals, traffic deaths, and AI that encourages potentially dangerous user behavior), we’re supposed to dig back in, assess the damage, and find ways to fix what we’ve broken. Even when unraveling the mess might itself seem impossible.

Right before I came to MIT Technology Review, I edited a newsletter about individual actions that can help address the climate crisis, which some would call—and have called—a fool’s errand, given the sheer scale of the problem. They might say it’s as implausible as an AI kill switch, practical nuclear fusion, or a superconductor that works at room temperature. But if I learned nothing else from three years spent finding ways for li’l old me (or li’l old you!) to chip away at one of humanity’s biggest existential threats, it’s that focusing on what we can’t do only makes the darkness darker.
So yeah, this one’s for the folks who have the audacity to try, and who refuse to let anyone—themselves included—tell them no.
I hope you enjoy the ride.
2ee0182f23a97c23: Just before the Artemis II crew began its historic slingshot around the moon this past April, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom. SR-1, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-­powered interplanetary spacecraft, is meant to fly an uncrewed mission to Mars by the end of 2028, arriving in 2029. A successful mission would herald a new era of more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight—saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation as they travel to Mars and beyond. “You wake up to that announcement, and it puts a big smile on your face,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales.

Running a nuclear reactor in space may sound like lunacy, but it’s not. The Soviet Union sent dozens of reactors into orbit, often to power spy satellites. And experts say there aren’t any major technical obstacles to making nuclear space propulsion happen. “I think it’s a very doable technology,” says Philip Metzger, a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute.“I’m happy to see them finally doing this.”

Still, developing space propulsion using reactors has been slow going. The US has started—and terminated—several programs looking into it over the past 75 years. The latest casualty was DRACO, a collaboration between NASA and the Department of Defense, which ended in 2025. The project was canceled because of high experimentation costs, an inability to compete with conventional rocket propulsion on price, and difficulty ensuring that ground tests could be performed safely and effectively. (You are creating an incredibly powerful nuclear reaction, after all.)

After much wavering, it now appears that nuclear-powered interplanetary travel is a $2 billion bet NASA is willing to make. The agency is pursuing an approach called nuclear electric propulsion, which uses the neutrons produced in a self-­sustaining, uranium-­atom-splitting reaction to create heat and ultimately electricity. The electricity is used to ionize a gas, which is blasted out of the spacecraft with the help of magnetic fields, generating thrust. The approach “is very low thrust, but very efficient,” says Sebastian Corbisiero, the US Department of Energy’s national technical director of space reactor programs. “So you can use it for a long period of time.”

What might such a rocket look like? A presentation by Steve Sinacore, program director of NASA’s SR-1 program, offers some clues. So far, the concept art makes the craft look like a colossal fletched arrow. The back will house the power-and-propulsion system, while the tip will hold a uranium-filled nuclear reactor with a capacity of at least 20 kilowatts. (For context, a typical nuclear plant on Earth is about 50,000 times more powerful.) The “fletches” on SR-1 are large fins that help cool the reactor by radiating heat into space.

Like many other pieces of space hardware, the reactor will need to be put through its paces on the ground before it’s cleared for the rough rocket trip to space. “Going through the launch safely is going to be a challenge,” says Middleburgh. “You are being shaken, rattled, and rolled.” For safety reasons, the reactor will be switched on around two days post-launch, when it’s comfortably far from Earth. Uranium isn’t tremendously dangerous by itself, but that can’t be said of the waste products that emerge when the reactor is running. If SR-1 works as planned, its journey to Mars will take about a year.

Will this novel form of space propulsion actually reach the Red Planet by 2029? It’s possible. NASA says the Idaho National Laboratory, which is building SR-1’s reactor, is making progress and is on target for a late-2028 launch. “Procurement of major components is underway, and integration work on the power and propulsion element is advancing steadily,” Sinacore told MIT Technology Review. The outlook will get even sunnier if the Artemis program, which aims to start laying the foundations for a base on the lunar south pole by the decade’s end, keeps to its own bold deadline.

“It’s an aggressive timeline,” says Lindsey Holmes, who is vice president of advanced projects at Analytical Mechanics Associates, an aerospace company in Virginia. She suspects the push is being driven partly by China’s and Russia’s own deep-space nuclear ambitions. The two countries have spoken about plans to place a reactor on the moon’s surface in the mid-2030s to power a jointly operated lunar base. Whether it flies or fails in space, SR-1’s development should help NASA put its own reactor on the moon; the technology involved in the two projects is broadly similar, given that the lunar surface, like space itself, is a vacuum. If an interplanetary nuclear-powered spacecraft works, a nuclear reactor on the moon should too.
Most of the technology for SR-1 already exists; it’s going to come down to piecing it all together and then seeing how it performs in space.
a25affc9ec1890c4: We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks—without the workout. The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who struggle with frailty, disability, or chronic illness.

It will take a lot of experimentation to untangle the myriad pathways by which exercise promotes health. But IDing the cascade of hormones, enzymes, and other molecules related to physical activity is just the first step. Scientists need to figure out how to turn that knowledge into safe and effective drugs. That’s a tall order: More than 90% of treatments that enter human studies fail.

There are regulatory hurdles too. The FDA approves medications to treat diseases, not to enhance wellness, says Thomas Burris, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida whose work focuses on diseases that respond to exercise, like obesity, type 2 diabetes, and dementia.

There may never be a pill that delivers all the benefits of exercise, but research could lead to new medicines that mimic some aspects of working out. Scientists have already identified many important exercise-related signals and have even developed compounds to regulate them. (Some preliminary results have been so promising that doping authorities have proactively banned the compounds.)

Burris and his colleagues are focused on a receptor that’s always switched on, even without exercise. Working out appears to boost that receptor in muscle cells, which in turn helps bolster endurance over time. Burris’s lab has spent years designing a drug that cranks up the receptor’s activity directly, and mice treated with the drug ran longer and farther than mice that weren’t. They “become marathon mice without having to do any type of exercise,” Burris says. There are even indications—also in mice—that the compound mimics some of the cognitive benefits of exercise and could help treat heart failure. Burris founded a company called Pelagos to carry the work forward into a clinical trial.

Other workout-mimicking drugs have already entered human studies. In June, the biotech firm Cambrian Bio reported that its experimental drug ATX-304 boosted metabolism and reduced liver and belly fat in people with obesity and prediabetes. It activates a metabolic switch that helps cells sense when energy supplies dip and coordinates the production of more fuel—the same switch that helps us sustain long sessions jumping rope or swimming laps. Cambrian hopes it will help people lose weight without losing muscle, a common concern with GLP-1 medicines.
Our understanding of how exercise benefits the body is still coming into focus, and drug development is prone to failure.
807cd6cdd4d4152d: From P Sundramoorthy

The high-profile investigation into the MBI International Group investment scheme raises a fundamental question about Malaysia’s response to major financial crime: what happens after arrests, raids, and the seizure or freezing of billions of ringgit in assets?
Under Op Northern Star, police announced the arrests of individuals suspected of facilitating the movement or laundering of funds linked to the alleged investment fraud.
By May 2025, authorities reported that 17 people were detained and assets worth approximately RM3.81 billion had been seized or frozen.
Subsequent reporting in January 2026 indicated that 23 people were arrested, with authorities pursuing the forfeiture of hundreds of properties and funds held in bank accounts.

These are significant developments. However, the public deserves clarity about whether investigations are progressing towards lawful outcomes and whether affected investors can realistically expect to recover their losses.
The MBI case should not be judged solely by the number of arrests or the value of assets seized. The real test is what follows.

Complex financial crime investigations require investigators to trace funds, establish individual responsibilities, examine corporate transactions and determine whether assets represent proceeds of unlawful activities.
The reported international dimension of the MBI case adds further challenges, including obtaining foreign evidence and coordinating with overseas enforcement agencies.

An arrest does not establish guilt, and a frozen asset does not automatically represent criminal proceeds. Similarly, release from remand does not necessarily mean a suspect has been cleared or that an investigation has ended.
However, these distinctions should not become a reason for prolonged public uncertainty.
Transparency without compromising investigations

When those previously detained in high-profile investigations return to their daily activities or retain prominent business and social positions, questions inevitably arise. Some may assume allegations have been dismissed, while others may suspect preferential treatment for influential individuals.

Neither conclusion should be drawn merely from a person's release or continued public presence. The presumption of innocence must be respected, and allegations must be established through proper legal proceedings.
The police should provide periodic updates while the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission should clarify the status of any related investigation within its jurisdiction.
Where legally permissible, updates should explain whether investigation papers have been referred to prosecutors and whether charges or asset forfeiture proceedings have commenced.

Where investigations have concluded or decisions have been made not to pursue particular individuals, appropriate clarification should be provided, subject to legal restrictions and the rights of those concerned.
Victims must not be forgotten

Perhaps the most important consideration is the position of investors who lost money through the MBI scheme. Announcements of billions of ringgit in seized or frozen assets may create expectations that investors will eventually recover their losses.
However, the value of seized assets does not necessarily represent the amount available for distribution to victims.
Assets may be subject to competing claims, ownership disputes and forfeiture proceedings. Their eventual recovery and distribution depend on applicable law and the outcomes of legal proceedings.
Authorities should communicate realistic expectations about asset recovery and explain, within legal limits, what mechanisms are available to address victims' claims.
Op Metal a broader lesson

The importance of following investigations through to their outcomes is also illustrated by Op Metal, a separate MACC operation launched in July 2025 targeting an alleged scrap metal and electronic waste smuggling syndicate.

Authorities seized assets worth over RM183 million and froze company and individual bank accounts containing approximately RM51 million. The suspected activities were estimated to have caused the government more than RM950 million in lost export tax revenue over six years.
Op Metal is unrelated to the MBI investment scheme investigation. However, it reinforces a broader lesson: seizures and enforcement announcements are only part of the process.

The MBI case warrants particular attention because of the financial losses suffered by investors and the importance of maintaining confidence in Malaysia's handling of major investment-related fraud allegations.
It presents an opportunity for Malaysian authorities to demonstrate that complex, cross-border financial crime can be confronted with determination, professionalism and transparency.
Ultimately, the public does not expect investigators to reveal everything, but it does expect them to explain what can responsibly be disclosed, demonstrate progress and communicate lawful outcomes.
Justice must extend beyond the headlines.
P Sundramoorthy is a criminologist at the Centre for Policy Research at Universiti Sains Malaysia and an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

7eac5dc4d24bb6eb: Malaysia's automotive industry has become an interesting battleground between Japan and China, two of the world's great carmaking powers. And the contest is being played out through our national carmakers, Proton and Perodua.
Proton has the backing of Zhejiang Geely, one of China's most technologically advanced automotive groups while Perodua has the support of Daihatsu and, behind it, the industrial might of Toyota.
Both partnerships have been successful, but the arrival of electric vehicles (EV) has changed the rules of the game.

China has taken a commanding lead in EV technology, battery production and manufacturing costs. Japan, despite its dominance of the global automotive industry for decades, has been more cautious about committing itself to battery electric vehicles beyond hybrids.
That puts Perodua in a particularly interesting position.

An important insight into Japan's intentions came in May when its ambassador to Malaysia, Noriyuki Shikata, described Perodua as one of the best examples of a successful Japanese-Malaysian joint venture. More significantly, he disclosed that Japan's economy, trade and industry ministry had decided to extend financial support for a new Perodua-led project.
Shikata also observed that Perodua was entering a new stage of innovation, developing solutions in Malaysia that Japan itself was interested in learning about.

Now, that is an interesting statement coming from the representative of one of the world's most sophisticated automotive nations. For more than three decades in the auto industry, we have regarded the Japanese as the teachers and Malaysians as the students.
Could the relationship now be evolving into something more equal?
From petrol to electric
Consider what Perodua has achieved.

Starting with the modest Kancil in 1994, it has grown into Malaysia's largest carmaker, commanding roughly 40% of our domestic market. Its success was built on affordable, reliable petrol-engine cars, efficient manufacturing and a formidable local supplier network.
The question is whether Perodua can translate these strengths into the electric age.

Its first home-grown EV, the QV-E, represents a bold but expensive undertaking. Unlike Proton, which can draw upon Geely's existing EV platforms and economies of scale, Perodua has invested heavily in developing its own product.
The difference is fundamental. Proton benefits from China's enormous EV ecosystem. Perodua is attempting to develop Malaysian engineering capabilities while building a new supply chain.
Market reception

The QV-E encountered a difficult market reception, with pricing and battery leasing arrangements initially raising questions among buyers. Subsequent price reductions have made it more competitive, but they also illustrate the formidable economics of EV manufacturing.
This is where government policy becomes important. Should Malaysia provide targeted financial assistance to Perodua to develop its EV capabilities?

I believe there is a strong case for doing so, provided the assistance is directed towards research, engineering, local components and technology development rather than simply subsidising car prices as China did for 5 years

There is an even stronger argument if Japan is prepared to participate. Toyota and Daihatsu possess enormous experience in manufacturing efficiency, quality control and supplier development. Combining these strengths with Perodua's local engineering ambitions could create something genuinely valuable.
It would also give Japan an opportunity to develop affordable EV technologies for Asean markets, where price sensitivity remains a major consideration.
Supply chains

We should not overlook that China already enjoys significant advantages in battery technology and scale. Perodua's QV-E itself uses batteries from China's CATL, among the world's biggest maker of EV batteries.
The modern automotive industry depends on international supply chains.
The objective should not be to manufacture every component in Malaysia. It should be to develop technologies and industrial capabilities in which Malaysians can become genuinely competitive.

Nor should this become another exercise in protecting a national carmaker from competition. The government must insist on measurable results, greater localisation, export potential and meaningful Malaysian intellectual property.
Green technology

The transition towards EVs should not be measured solely by the number of electric vehicles sold. The environmental impact of automotive manufacturing, energy consumption, battery production, material sourcing and recycling must also be considered.
Government R&D assistance should therefore include the development and adoption of green technologies and cleaner manufacturing processes throughout Malaysia's automotive industry.
This could include energy-efficient production systems, AI-based energy optimisation, battery recycling, resource efficiency and technologies that reduce industrial emissions.
Such initiatives would not only support environmental sustainability but also improve the competitiveness of Malaysian automotive suppliers in international markets.
Measurable benefits

A proper mechanism should be established to assess the actual national benefits generated by government R&D assistance. Malaysia's New Incentive Framework, introduced in 2026, already moves towards linking investment incentives with measurable economic outcomes.

Rather than creating overlapping subsidy schemes, the government should examine how existing mechanisms can be strengthened and better coordinated to support automotive AI, strategic R&D and green industrial development.
The Japanese ambassador's remarks suggest that Japan sees something worth supporting in Perodua. Malaysia should recognise the opportunity.
Rather than viewing Proton and Perodua simply as two national carmakers competing for domestic sales, perhaps we should see them as two different pathways into the future of automotive manufacturing.
One draws upon China's extraordinary scale and speed. The other could build upon Japan's engineering discipline and Malaysia's own industrial experience.
If both succeed, Malaysia will be the winner. And the one which exports the most is the champion.

9a892035dd55c082: From Shahrim Tamrin
I welcome Malaysian Institute of Road Safety Research (Miros) chairman Wong Shaw Voon’s renewed call to raise the minimum age for a motorcycle licence from 16 to 18.
But this is hardly a new proposal. It has been under discussion since 2018.
Malaysia needs neither another round of deliberations nor another announcement without a clear outcome. It needs transparency, a policy decision and the political will to act.

In May 2018, during Loke Siew Fook’s first term as transport minister, the transport ministry sought public feedback on the minimum licensing age, with Miros and relevant road safety authorities involved. The exercise ran until September, but its findings have never been made publicly available through official channels.

I obtained a summary of Miros’s findings after requesting it two years ago. The results were mixed. The online exercise involved 4,005 members of the public and 11 experts, while a separate survey covered 4,158 respondents.

Although Miros reported majority support among online participants for raising the age to 18, many motorcycle riders and secondary school students opposed the change. Some students even suggested lowering the age.
The findings do not establish a blanket public mandate for change. They establish something more fundamental: evidence was collected and the public deserves to know what became of it.

The presentation also reported that 80% of boys and 86% of girls surveyed rode to school without a motorcycle licence. Of 181 boys aged 16, only three held one. Meanwhile, 58% of students said their parents did not stop them from riding.

These figures concern the students surveyed, not all Malaysian schoolchildren. Nevertheless, they expose a problem that raising the licensing age alone cannot solve. Even a 13-year-old can ride an illegally obtained “kapcai”.
Wong himself has cautioned that raising the age will achieve little without effective enforcement against underage riders.
Licensing reform must, therefore, go hand in hand with enforcement, parental accountability and controls over access to motorcycles.
The paper trail

On Oct 8, 2019, police proposed a new B3 motorcycle licensing category at the National Road Safety Council’s 60th annual general meeting. The proposal envisaged restricting young riders to motorcycles of 70cc or below, or low-powered electric alternatives, to curb illegal street racing and improve road safety.

Recorded as Item 9.4 in the meeting minutes, the proposal was referred to the transport ministry. Years later, the public is still waiting to learn whether it was seriously considered and why it produced no clear policy outcome.

On Nov 25, 2021, Miros’s board backed a related but distinct proposal to study restricting young riders to motorcycles below 90cc. Recorded as Board Paper LPM 2-52 under Item 52.4(2), it was approved by the board, including its then chairman Suret Singh.
One proposal concerned a licensing category; the other concerned research into engine-capacity restrictions.
Nearly five years later, the study’s status remains unclear. Was it completed? What did it find? Were recommendations submitted to the transport ministry? If the study was not completed, why not?

In August 2024, the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia (Suhakam) children’s commissioner Farah Nini Dusuki sought an update on the B3 proposal and urged the transport ministry and road transport department (JPJ) to expedite legislation addressing motorcycle purchases by unlicensed riders. She also highlighted the unresolved status of the Miros study.
A study endorsed by the board should not become an administrative mystery.
Human cost
Suhakam has highlighted the risks faced by underage motorcyclists, including 87 children aged six to 10 who died while riding motorcycles rather than as pillion passengers.
Children do not acquire motorcycles by themselves. Adults may purchase them, provide access or knowingly permit illegal riding. Sellers and the wider regulatory framework also warrant scrutiny.

Section 31(1)(a) of the Child Act 2001 addresses neglect likely to cause physical injury to a child, while Section 39(5) of the Road Transport Act 1987 addresses causing or permitting a child below 16 to drive. Their application depends on the circumstances and relevant legal requirements.
Parental accountability matters, but it must not become a substitute for institutional accountability.

The government should disclose the status of legislation reportedly being developed to regulate motorcycle purchases by unlicensed individuals, explain outstanding obstacles and provide a timetable. The problem extends beyond teenagers riding kapcai – unlicensed adults can also access more powerful motorcycles.
I call on the transport ministry, JPJ and Miros to:
Publish the 2018 survey. Release its methodology, detailed findings and recommendations, while protecting respondents’ personal information where necessary.
Account for Board Paper LPM 2-52. Confirm whether the study was completed, publish its findings and explain what action followed.
Disclose the proposed legislation’s status. Set a timetable for regulating motorcycle purchases by unlicensed buyers and establish enforceable safeguards.

Set a timetable for licensing reform. Decide whether to raise the minimum age to 18 and seriously consider the B3 proposal, alongside proportionate power restrictions for young and inexperienced riders, effective enforcement and meaningful parental accountability.
Wong deserves credit for returning the issue to the agenda. In my years covering Miros, I have seen board recommendations stall before reaching the ministerial table.
It remains unclear whether Board Paper LPM 2-52, or any recommendation arising from it, ever reached the transport minister in a form requiring a decision. That, too, warrants an explanation.

Research cannot improve road safety if recommendations fail to travel from the boardroom to the ministerial table. Nor can policy succeed if it exists only in announcements, meeting minutes and presentation slides.
Malaysia is not short of studies, recommendations or press statements. It is short of visible follow-through.
Publish the evidence. Account for the decisions made and those left unmade. Set a timetable and act. The public has waited long enough, and too many children have already paid the price.
Shahrim Tamrin is a sustainable transport and road safety activist and former Malaysian Institute of Road Safety Research board member.

7a9898c01ede12be: If Bersama were to contest 15 seats in the Melaka polls on Nov 14, it is certain to take away votes from PKR, DAP and Amanah.

It is not too late to rescind a move that bodes ill for a future in which Bersama ought to have a vital role in making the reforms long sought by Pakatan Harapan (PH) a reality, thereby setting on course the creation of a different country from the prevailing one, whose contours are likely to be reinforced by the right-wingers of Umno and the Islamists of PAS.

As if the good fairies have decided to play a hand in steering things towards an outcome both congenial for Bersama and beneficial to PH, Bersama’s co-founder Nik Nazmi Nik Ahmad is in a spot of bother that may well throw him off stride for GE16.

The khalwat case he is facing may well disqualify the former MP for Setiawangsa from being the constituency’s first Bersama MP at GE16. Prior to the case’s inception, Nik Nazmi was on course, after resigning as PKR MP for Setiawangsa, to being returned at GE16, under Bersama’s colours, as the seat’s MP.
Now that probability is dimmed by what hangs over him at the shariah court.

This is grist for the argument that Bersama ought to draw in its tentacles and play to its strengths. There is no point in splitting votes at the Melaka polls and persisting in attacking PKR and Anwar Ibrahim on the stumps, as Bersama has been known to do from the time the party set sail.

When Rafizi Ramli and Nik Nazmi launched a new political vehicle by forming Bersama, it was clear the pair were on course, heading up to GE16, which must be called by February 2028, to carve off something like 10 of the 31 parliamentary seats that PKR won at GE15 in November 2022.
Their incumbents were pro-Rafizi and will likely be won again by the same coterie if re-contested by them.
Bersama will want to contest a number of other seats held by PKR MPs, but not significantly more.

Bersama went into the Johor state polls in July with hopes of making some gains. They wound up with nothing but lost deposits and were suitably chagrined to not want to contest in the subsequent Negeri Sembilan polls.
But now Bersama fancies its chances in Melaka: it has not learnt its lesson that what plays in the Klang Valley does not exactly play outside its highly urban and urbane precincts.
The Nik Nazmi khalwat case is a symptom of Bersama’s presumptuousness.
The party must play within its strengths.
And wait for the realisation to congeal that after Anwar, it is Rafizi who should resuscitate the fallen reformasi colours.
Hence, there isn’t much point in alienating its putative allies in PKR, DAP and Amanah by going solo and splitting votes at the Melaka polls and elsewhere.
What has happened to Nik Nazmi should introduce some grains of sand into Bersama’s balm of complacent assumption.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.

6c941b9db65caba4: Hidup berjiran memang ada macam-macam ragam.

Ada jiran yang baik hati, suka menolong, ringan tulang dan mengambil berat tentang orang sekeliling. Ada juga jiran yang kita tidak begitu kenal, tetapi tidak pernah mendatangkan masalah. Masing-masing menjaga hal sendiri.
Ada yang sudah bertahun-tahun tinggal berdepan-depan, tetapi sekadar angkat tangan dan senyum. Tidak pernah berbual. Janji tidak menyusahkan orang lain, kita baik-baik sahaja.
Ada juga yang langsung tidak mahu memandang, apatah lagi bertegur sapa. Tetapi selagi tidak membuat susah kepada orang lain, itu pun tidak mengapa.
Yang susah apabila mendapat jiran yang selalu buat hal. Entah apa penyakitnya, suka membuat orang lain tidak senang.
Laman rumahnya bersemak-samun sehingga mungkin menjadi tempat pembiakan nyamuk. Ditambah pula suka membuat bising tidak mengenal waktu. Sudah tentu kita semua akan rimas dan serba salah.
Apabila ditegur, dia tidak berubah. Silap-silap kita pula diajak bertumbuk.

Bukan dia sahaja yang menyusahkan, seluruh keluarganya pun sama. Anak-anak bukan main nakal, suka mengganggu rakan sebaya. Emaknya pula bermulut jahat, suka mengata sana-sini. Tidak boleh tengok orang lain lebih sedikit, dinaikkan pula hantaran menyindir di media sosial.

Lama-kelamaan, seluruh kejiranan bengang dan terganggu dengan perangai jiran seperti ini sehingga masalah itu terpaksa dibawa ke mesyuarat persatuan penduduk, malah memerlukan campur tangan ketua masyarakat atau pihak berkuasa.
Tetapi masalah tetap tidak selesai. Dia masih tidak berubah.
Apabila ada pihak datang sebagai wakil pendamai untuk memujuk, pandai pula dia mengajar orang lain. Disuruhnya kita bersabar. Katanya, hidup berjiran perlu ada toleransi.

Kemudian dia merengek dan berlakon menjadi mangsa. Orang lain semuanya salah, dia sahaja yang betul. Disebut-sebut dan diungkit-ungkit pula apa yang sudah dilakukannya selama ini. Kononnya dia juga ada jasa di kawasan kejiranan.
Ini bukan cerita rekaan.
Kalau kita tinggal di kampung, rumah pangsa rakyat atau taman perumahan, memang ada orang jenis begini. Kadang-kadang kita pun tidak faham bagaimana orang seperti mereka boleh wujud di muka bumi ini.
Ketika orang lain sepakat dan boleh hidup aman, dia muncul mengocak ketenangan. Apa kepuasan yang dia dapat, kita pun tidak boleh hendak hadam.
Takkanlah tidak tahu bahawa dalam beragama memang ada bab adab hidup berjiran. Kita dituntut supaya menghormati jiran, menjaga hubungan baik dan tidak menyusahkan orang lain.

Tetapi hubungan baik sepatutnya berjalan dua hala. Tidak bolehlah seorang jiran sentiasa diminta bersabar sedangkan jiran yang menyebabkan masalah sewenang-wenangnya melakukan apa sahaja yang dia suka.
Hal-hal mudah pun sepatutnya kita boleh fikir sendiri.
Jangan halang pintu keluar masuk rumah jiran dengan kereta kita. Jangan biarkan haiwan peliharaan membuang najis merata-rata di atas jalan atau di rumah jiran.
Pada musim perayaan, kalau boleh elakkan membakar mercun apabila sudah masuk waktu tidur. Ada anak kecil dan orang tua yang tidak sihat, pasti mereka akan terkejut.
Jangan pula bakar sampah sehingga asap masuk ke rumah jiran.
Ini semua perkara yang kita boleh fikir sendiri.
Tetapi nanti sekejap.
Bagaimana kalau mereka sebenarnya tahu perbuatan itu menyusahkan orang lain, tetapi tidak mempedulikannya?
Lebih teruk lagi jika mereka mendapat keuntungan daripada perbuatan itu, sedangkan orang lain terpaksa menanggung akibatnya.
Ini bukan lagi soal kesedaran atau common sense. Ini sudah masuk soal tanggungjawab.
Rasulullah SAW bersabda, maksudnya:
“Demi Allah, tidak beriman! Demi Allah, tidak beriman! Demi Allah, tidak beriman!”
Apabila ditanya siapakah orang itu, Baginda menjawab:
“Orang yang jirannya tidak berasa aman daripada gangguannya.”
(Riwayat al-Bukhari, no. 6016)

Apabila dikatakan jiran, ia jelas tidak terbatas kepada kaum dan agama. Jiran ialah mereka yang paling dekat di sekeliling kita, yang bersama-sama menjadi sebahagian daripada sesebuah kelompok atau komuniti.
Begitulah Islam mementingkan kesejahteraan jiran tetangga. Kita dituntut berbuat baik kepada jiran walaupun berbeza warna kulit dan kepercayaan.
Tetapi watak pengacau tetap ada.
Bukan di rumah sahaja. Di dalam bilik darjah, pasti ada seorang watak pengacau atau kaki buli. Di pejabat pula ada kaki mengadu domba.
Malah, di peringkat dunia pun ada negara yang kita panggil jiran tetapi suka buat hal.
Tiap-tiap tahun rumah kita dimasuki asap gara-gara jiran membuat pembakaran “di halamannya”. Kita dan jiran-jiran lain sudah puas mengeluh, tetapi dia tidak peduli.
Apa kita hendak buat dengan mereka?
Sikap tidak mempedulikan pihak lain ini cukup membuatkan kita tertekan. Kita bingung dan mati kutu. Sampai bilakah keadaan ini akan berterusan? Bilakah pula mereka akan sedar dan berubah?
Maka, setelah puas mengeluh, ayuhlah kita berdoa kepada tuhan agar pintu akal mereka terbuka dan mereka menjadi lebih bijak sedikit.
Berdoalah sungguh-sungguh sebelum terlambat. Sebelum keamanan dan kesihatan kita musnah.
Bukan apa.
Saya sudah bosan dengan jerebu ini.

773c6020d7b35831: From Moaz Nair
Not too long ago, Negeri Sembilan stood proud as a bastion of political tranquillity amidst a turbulent national landscape.

Under the previous Barisan Nasional–Pakatan Harapan coalition government led by former menteri besar Aminuddin Harun, the state enjoyed a rare commodity in modern Malaysian politics: absolute administrative stability.

Today, that hard-won stability has been recklessly squandered. Negeri Sembilan now finds itself ensnared in a historic, multi-layered constitutional crisis born entirely of the current government’s own missteps.

For the voters, legal experts, and everyday citizens witnessing this paralysis, the contrast between past order and present dysfunction could not be starker. The memory of the previous BN-PH framework is fast becoming the definitive benchmark for stable governance and a bitter reminder of how far the state has fallen.

The crowning achievement of the previous administration was its meticulous commitment to preserving constitutional harmony and institutional traditions. Negeri Sembilan’s governance model is uniquely complex, relying on a centuries-old, delicate equilibrium between a modern elected executive, the monarchy, and the state’s sacred, uncodified Adat Perpatih (customary law) institutions.

Aminuddin’s government managed this sensitive balance not by luck, but through sheer political maturity and institutional restraint. Recognising the vital need to insulate daily partisan politics from royal affairs, his government maintained a peaceful, respectful coexistence between elected officials, the Undang Yang Empat (traditional chieftains), and the Yang Dipertuan Besar.
Mutual respect
It was a partnership built on mutual respect and systemic boundaries, ensuring that time-honoured traditions and modern democracy reinforced rather than undermined one another.

Crucially, this political maturity served as a protective shield that insulated the state from systemic crises. Backers of the previous government frequently note that the coalition successfully shielded the civil service and state apparatus from being dragged into protracted constitutional disputes.

Today, we realise just how vital that bulwark was, and how easily it could be dismantled by naked political opportunism. The moment the BN-PH cooperation fractured, it triggered an unprecedented and destructive chain reaction that has shaken the state to its core.

The descent into absolute turmoil accelerated rapidly last April, when 14 BN assemblymen abruptly withdrew their support from Aminuddin’s government following a dispute involving royal affairs. Rather than prioritising state stability, this drastic move plunged the state into a perilous political vacuum, leaving a minority government in its wake and forcing a snap election.

This vacuum did more than just disrupt daily executive governance; it threw open the doors to the current existential crisis— an unprecedented, overt succession dispute between Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir and Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar, who is backed by the current administration.
Constitutional deadlock
The collapse of the foundational political consensus has dragged the state legislative assembly into a complex, multi-layered constitutional deadlock with no clear legal exit ramp.

We are now forced to witness an extraordinary and embarrassing clash of powers. In direct response to aggressive moves by the new state executive council supporting a proclamation to depose him, Tuanku Muhriz took the radical but decisive step of revoking the appointments of all 10 state executive councillors. Citing a direct breach of their oaths of office, the palace purged the state cabinet in one swift stroke.

The fallout has left governance not just shaky, but completely paralysed. The current menteri besar, Ismail Lasim, now stands isolated—a lone captain aboard a ghost ship. In a bizarre attempt to downplay this structural damage, Ismail has chosen to prioritise appointing village chiefs and village development and security committees rather than resolving the critical vacancies in his cabinet.

To claim that state administration is "running smoothly" while the formal sitting of the state assembly has been indefinitely postponed until late November is an insult to the voters' intelligence. This represents a profound failure of the democratic apparatus, where grassroots local appointments are being deployed as a smoke screen to mask a total absence of executive authority.
Painful lesson

Negeri Sembilan is learning a painful lesson first-hand: when you dismantle a functional political consensus for short-term gain, the alternative is rarely better. The current turmoil proves that the previous BN-PH ruling alliance was not merely a marriage of convenience — it was a vital stabilising force.

The current menteri besar cannot continue to govern in a state of absolute paralysis, pretending that village-level appointments can substitute for a functioning state legislative assembly or a complete Exco line-up.

The state’s political leaders must urgently put aside partisan egos, halt their dangerous chess game against traditional institutions, and return to the constitutional blueprint that guaranteed peace for years. The state's executive vacuum is no longer an isolated political squabble; it is a systemic crisis threatening the very fabric of Negeri Sembilan’s unique identity.
If the current leadership is incapable of restoring the stable, respectful equilibrium of the past, they must accept their failure and step aside for those who can.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

5896ab894451fee5: Over the Merdeka holidays, I went fishing with some friends off the Pahang and Johor coast. We started off from the Kuala Rompin jetties on a lovely morning with mist shrouding the mangrove and hovering over the river. It was a beautiful, peaceful sight.

Then the sun started getting hotter but the mist remained… and remained, acting in a most un-misty way. When we sailed away from the river mouth we could still see this “mist” all around us. It wasn’t mist. It was the haze, right there on the east coast hundreds of kilometres from the nearest Indonesian territories, yet enough of it was visible even in Pulau Tioman.

Over the last few months, I've been saying “I've never seen haze this bad, only to update it again multiple times on subsequent days. The haze last week was especially bad, but I’m sure as records go this too will be broken soon.

What can I say about the haze that hasn’t been said by many for years? I’m relatively healthy for my age and don’t have any bad allergy problems, but I still get headaches and nausea because of it. I can’t bear to think about what those with actual health issues must be going through.
The current haze seems worse than previous ones. It hangs heavy and feels thick and foul, often covering the sun and hills and gloomily blocking vision to barely a kilometre or so on the highway.

Everybody is frustrated with it, including an Indonesian official who slammed his Malaysian and Singaporean neighbours for complaining about the haze from Sumatra without acknowledging it also gives us oxygen during better days.

Hello! Our Indonesian official friend forgets his high school chemistry. Sumatra is passing us more than oxygen now, this time the said oxygen is all bound up with carbon and sulphur and nitrogen and other elements to form noxious and poisonous monoxides and dioxides and ozone!
Not exactly the kind of trade among friends. After decades of “importing” this stuff for months most years, we deserve a breather, if you’ll pardon the expression.
The Indonesians are also experimenting with clearing the haze with dry ice, which is supposed to lift the smoke particles higher into the atmosphere and clear the land.

Great – now the smoke particles will go even higher into the Indonesian skies to catch the stronger monsoon wind up there and even more of them can waft their way to Malaysia. Thank you again Indonesia!

In reality, Indonesia’s forest fire problem has gotten out of hand. The fires have literally gone underground, setting off the uncontrollable burning of dry underground peat. Once this catches fire, only the deluge of a monsoon can put it out.

This year a combination of factors, including a more severe El Nino, is exacerbating the problem; perhaps a madder-than-usual rush to burn forests, because there’s less of them left every year, is making things worse.

What we need to see is a more aggressive attitude among the political leaders of the region in fighting this menace. Our own leaders must also start demanding more be done by Indonesia to stop this perennial curse.

Of the culprits setting the forest on fire in Sumatra and Kalimantan are believed to include some big Malaysian plantation companies. If that is so, bring them to account and throw the book at them: I can guarantee there’ll be loud cheers from us ordinary Malaysians.
And ordinary Indonesians too. If it’s bad for us hundreds of kilometres away from the worst of it, just imagine how bad it must be for the unfortunate people living right there.

They can't go fishing away from the haze, like I did. They can’t get into private jets and fly out of the country to foreign clearer skies, as some people did. They just have to stay there and suck it all in literally and suffer now and/or die earlier later.

Our problems are not with the ordinary Indonesians, many of whom suffer even worse than us because of this haze. Our issues are with the Indonesian authorities who we don’t see treating the problem as the emergency it actually is.
And our issue is also with our own leaders who are more interested in maintaining peace and harmony while our people are literally choking with illness and maybe even death.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
